subtopic: RETURN TO THE HOUSE AFTER ABSENCE THROUGH ILLNESS-ANNOUNCEMENT AS TO VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: RETURN TO THE HOUSE AFTER ABSENCE THROUGH ILLNESS-ANNOUNCEMENT AS TO VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with your permission I rise to speak on behalf of my associates; indeed, on this occasion I trust I speak for the whole house when I express to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) a warm welcome upon his return. I am sure we are all pleased to see him looking so well, and we trust that he is as well as he looks. If either now or in the future he should require any further rest, I am sure also that it will be readily given by every section of the house. Judging from his appearance, I gather he does not need one. His ruddy complexion would indicate that the sunshine of Virginia has done him more good than the storms in the House of Commons have done the rest of us.
I am happy to be able to assure him that in his absence the house was most competently led by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent). Sometimes he and his associates were right in their attitude toward the public questions which came before us; always, when they were right they had the support of those of us on this side of the house. But sometimes both he and his associates were wrong, and on those occasions we did our best to get them back on the right trail.
I am sure I speak for all hon. members when I say we are glad to see the Prime Minister back, and we trust his condition is such that he may carry on his duties here without any danger of further impairment of his health.

subtopic: RETURN TO THE HOUSE AFTER ABSENCE THROUGH ILLNESS-ANNOUNCEMENT AS TO VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise not because the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) is not speaking in this matter for this group as well as for his own, but to add my expression of personal pleasure at seeing the Prime Minister back in his place, and to express the hope

The Prime Minister
that he may long be spared to fill that position, or, if not, some other position in the house.
I would also associate myself with tire leader of the opposition in his reference to the acting leader of the house during the Prime Minister's absence. I think I am not speaking too strongly when I say that during that time he has endeared himself to hon. members in all parts of the house.
Mr. SOLON E. LOW (Peace River): Mr. Speaker, I am sure we share the sentiments expressed by the leader of the opposition and the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis). We are happy to see the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) back in his place.
During his absence I believe we did a pretty good job; the amount of business transacted was, I should think, quite satisfactory. Of course we are not hoping that the Prime Minister may have to go again soon, so that.we can do more; but I am suggesting that we took his advice and carried on quite well in his absence. We hope his health will continue to be good, so that he may not be forced to go away again.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: RETURN TO THE HOUSE AFTER ABSENCE THROUGH ILLNESS-ANNOUNCEMENT AS TO VISIT OF PRESIDENT OF THE UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I thank most warmly my hon. friend the leader of the opposition and the hon. gentlemen who have spoken for other parties on the opposite side of the house and the members of their parties, for the kind welcome they have extended to me; and may I also extend to all my fellow members on this side of the house my warmest thanks also for the manner in which they received the words of hon. members opposite.
I need not say how delighted I am to be back in the House of Commons. My little trip to the south has done me a lot of good. I felt considerably in need of a rest before going away; but I have come back feeling greatly benefited by it, and I hope from now on in the proceedings of the house I shall be able to pull my full weight in the boat.
While the weather in the south was a bit inclement, I gather it was not quite as bad as it was here. However that is all more than compensated for by what hon. gentlemen opposite have been saying about the progress that has been made in the business of the house in the last few weeks.
May I join with those who have spoken of my colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in expressing to him my warmest thanks for the manner in which he
has led the house during my absence and for the example which he has set to all its members, including myself.
I should like also to express a word of warm appreciation to the members of the press gallery and other friends who greeted me so cordially on my arrival back in the city on Saturday afternoon, and a word of very sincere appreciation of the many courtesies extended to me while I was in the United States, particularly by the government of the United States.
I am happy to be able to inform the house that the President, Mr. Truman, has definitely accepted the invitation of the Governor General and the government to visit our capital, probably in June, and that Mrs. Truman will also accompany him. The President expressed to me the hope and expectation that he and Mrs. Truman would be accompanied by their daughter. I gave to the President the assurance, which was unnecessary, that he and the members of his family would receive a very warm welcome from the citizens of Canada.

speechtext:
1.	What aid, if any, has been given towards alleviating the food shortage and famine in Great Britain caused by recent floods and storms, and to the economic strain brought about by the recent -war?

Mr. ST. LAURENT:
1.	The need for special help from overseas to alleviate shortages caused by the recent floods and storms in the British isles, is a matter which the Lbiited Kingdom government
will wish to consider itself. Up to the present time the Canadian government has no information which would indicate that the United Kingdom is contemplating any request for such help. For the purpose of alleviating economic strain brought about by the recent war, the Canadian government in 1946 extended a credit of one and one-quarter billion dollars to the United Kingdom. In addition, the long term contracts entered into by the United Kingdom and Canadian governments will do much to facilitate the import of foodstuffs into the United Kingdom.
2.	The advisability of charging the cost of privately dispatched relief parcels against the Canadian dollar credit is a matter for the United Kingdom government itself to decide.
3.	The postage charges on parcels to the United Kingdom are made up of three separate arrangements: (a) Charges for conveyance in Canada which are paid at so much per pound ; (b) Charges of the shipping companies for conveyance at sea, which are paid on the basis of cubic space occupied; (c) Charges of the general post office in the United Kingdom, which are paid at so much per pound.
Parcel post shipments are not calculated on a bulk basis, and no comparison is possible.

subtopic: IMMIGRATION-POLISH SOLDIERS
IMMIGRATION-POLISH SOLDIERS
speechtext:
1.	Does the British government provide shipping space as well as fares for another hatch of Polish soldiers for whom a team has already gone over?
Questions

2.	Did any of these soldiers fight against Britain in the last war and where?
3.	What branch of the Polish army did they belong to, and did any of them fight with Germany in the last war on the western or Italian front?
4.	Wliat check is there by Canada of these soldiers and what is the nature of the agreement with Britain to accept them, and to what number, and on what terms, and to what provinces will this contingent be assigned and for what work?
Mr. ST. LAURENT:
1.	Yes.
2.	Some of them were conscripted into the German army and fought on the Italian front and in north west Europe.
3.	They belonged to those formations of the Polish army serving under British command. The question whether any of them fought with Germany on the western or Italian front is answered by Nos. 2 and 4.
4.	Selection is made by a team of Canadian government officials composed of representatives of the Departments of Agriculture and Labour and the R.C.M.P.
The Canadian overseas medical immigration service provides the necessary doctors to carry out the medical examinations. Only those are accepted who are medically fit, took part in active hostilities against the axis powers and also qualify under the terms of the agreement with the United Kingdom. Those who participated voluntarily in hostilities on the side of the axis, or who have criminal records, are rejected.
The agreement with the United Kingdom provides that Canada will permit entry into this country of 4,000 Polish veterans who served with the allied forces engaged in hostilities against the axis powers, who are single and who are qualified for and willing to undertake agricultural employment in Canada. The United Kingdom has agreed that the Canadian government will make the selection of those who have applied and an undertaking will be signed by the successful applicant by which he agrees to accept farm labour at current wage rates and in accordance with living and working conditions prevailing in the locality of his employment, and will continue in agricultural employment for a period of two years. There is provision in the agreements for the return to the United Kingdom within two years of any individual who might be found to be unsuitable.
Further details are contained in the statement made to the house on this topic by the Secretary of State for External Affairs on July 25, 1946, and reported in Hansard pages 3836 and 3838 and in order in council P.C. 3112 of July 23, 1946, which was tabled at the same time.
fMr. Church.]

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. GLEN (Minister of Mines and Resources):
speechtext: The hon. member spoke to me before I came into the house regarding this matter. This man came to Canada's shores some time ago-I have not the date, and I had no opportunity of looking at the file. He came as a seaman or second officer on board ship, landed in Canada, and said that he was here for the purpose of reshipping, which he did not do. After some time he made application for permanent landing in Canada. His case was heard and refused. He appealed to me and I again refused, because he is not admissible under the regulations. Hon. DOUGLAS ABBOTT (Minister of Finance) moved that the house go into supply.

I have a few words to say before the house resolves itself into committee of supply. The government is asking the house to vote supply of funds. In accordance with established British custom, I rise to voice a grievance, to make a request for redress, and later perhaps to offer an alternative. My grievance is that the income tax in my riding of Lethbridge and throughout the other 243 ridings of Canada is an irksome and injurious burden. A tax on all income between $660 and $3,000 is destroying the incentive of Canadian youth to acquire additional education, to marry and make homes and to have babies urgently needed in Canada. It is destroying incentive to be loyal and stable citizens devoted to Canadian democracy, and confident in Canada's future.
Income taxes are destroying the incentive of all Canadian producers to produce both goods and services. Income taxes are impairing both incentive and ability of Canadian consumers to consume both goods and services. Furthermore income taxes, by decreas-

Income Tax-Exemptions
mg pm-chasing power just exactly where purchasing power should be increased, are greasing the skids and preparing for a headlong plunge of the Canadian economy down the ways into the gloomy seas of depression.
The redress I request is that in his forthcoming budget the Minister of Finance exempt from income tax for single people all incomes of $1,500 and under; for married people all incomes of $3,000 a year and under.
The last speech I delivered in the house was on old age pensions. In that speech I requested that $50 a month be given to people sixty-five years of age and over with no means test, with free hospitalization, medical and dental services. I can conceive that the Minister of Finance may say: Where is the money coming from? How, he will say, can the hon. member claim to be consistent when he makes speeches of this kind so close together?
May I repeat what the people of Canada and this house must learn, that our ability to produce goods and to provide services determines our ability to pay old age pensions or to do anything else we choose to do. Our ability to have money ought to depend on our productive capacity as to goods and services. During the war it was commonly said and generally accepted in government circles that Canada's performance in the war would depend entirely upon her resources, human and material. The same thing should be true in time of peace. Our ability to perform should depend on our ability to produce goods and services.
I suggest to the minister that he should begin to consider an alternative to the financial methods which he is using which are doing so much damage to the Canadian people. I suggest that the minister so change the financial system of Canada as to enable that financial system to render financially possible for Canadians, that level of living standards which Canada's resources, human and material, make physically possible. Such a change can be discovered, Mr. Speaker. It can be made by the government of the day. Such a change ought to be made forthwith before serious deterioration, threatening us at the present time in Canada, sets in in real earnest. Such a change must be made if Canadians are to avoid disasters in the near future.
I have no need to draw hon. members' attention to the rapid development of communism in this country. I have no need to point out how restless labouring people are becoming, considering the dangerous rise in prices. I have no need to hint at disruptive
disorders which might follow. We might have far worse than all of these unless something is done, and done soon.
The change, if efficacious, must go far deeper than any possible expansion of Canada's foreign trade policy. It must go far deeper than any modification or combination of modifications of heretofore accepted principles of trade, either external or internal, or both together.
How it has come about that the peoples of the Anglo-Saxon world have become so much obsessed with the idea that the only thing they can do to increase their prosperity is to trade more is something which it is beyond my ability to understand. Take the United States for example, consisting of forty-eight states. In effect they are forty-eight nations. Now, if trade could solve their problems they could trade among themselves and solve those problems. But they do not find themselves able to do so. That fact ought to be sufficient to warn all hon. members that the mere expansion of trade will not provide the remedy we must have for the economic ills that beset us.
The change which is necessary in our system must be widely different from any kind or degree of governmental or social ownership of the means of production such as our soeialis-tically inclined friends seem to be enamoured of. The change must comprise a fundamental change in technique in our financial system.
I suggest to the minister that he earnestly study "Economic Tribulation" by Vincent C. Vickers, published in 1941, and printed by Stephen Austin and Sons Limited in Hertford, England. So that all those who are interested may realize that there are men not such crackpots as social creditors are supposed to be-that there are really men of affairs who have achieved a standing who are confident that something can be done with the financial system, may I quote from this book. Vickers, in his foreword, at page 1, has this to say:
Ever since that day in 1926 when, not in arrogance but with humility, I felt it my duty to explain to the governor of the Bank of England, Mr. Montagu Norman, that "henceforth I was going to fight him and the gold standard and the Bank of England policy until I die"- (and well I remember the words of his reply!) -I have been an ardent money reformer. Some few years afterwards I resigned my long directorship of Vickers Limited; since when I have spent much time and money in advocating the necessity for a reform of the monetary system.
Further on in the foreword he says:
I bear no ill-feeling towards my own class or any other class. I seek neither notoriety nor kudos. If someone can change my convictions I shall be only too ready to alter them. But in
Income Tax-Exemptions

fifteen years nothing whatever has occurred to make me alter my views. I still believe that the existing system is actively harmful to the state, creates poverty and unemployment, and is the root cause of war. This personal confession is merely to demonstrate that I have seen both sides of the picture. My opinions are based upon my own experience and knowledge. I am today in the unique position of being absolutely and entirely devoid of animosity and wholly disinterested. I feel myself no longer under any restrictions whatsoever, except to guard against doing harm to my country or giving offence to anyone.
May I say a word or two regarding this man. Here is a man who had been a director of the Bank of England, who had been high in the directorate of Vickers, a great industrial organization. Here is a man who certainly ought not to be disregarded when he speaks so learnedly and so earnestly concerning a matter of such vital importance.
I will not detain the house longer except to read two or three statements which Vincent Vickers makes in the concluding chapter of his book, at page 74, in the chapter headed "The Direction of Future Policy". In recommendation No. 1 he advocates:
State control and state issue of currency and credit through a central organization managed and controlled by the state.
I see the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley), the former minister of finance, in his place. I think the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) would be well advised to read that book and to avoid thinking all the things that the present Minister of Justice has said about inflation resulting from debt-free money created by the state. Here in Mr. Vickers is a man of high orthodox authority who solemnly advocates debt free money. I will not read all his recommendations because I wish to save the time of the house. Recommendation No. 4, however, reads:
Any additional supply of money should be issued as a clear asset to the state; so that money will be spent into existence, and not lent into existence.
Whereby, of course, anyone can see that this man advocates what social erediters have advocated these many years, namely, debt-free money:
5.	The fluctuating quantity of gold lying in the vaults of the banking system should never be permitted to govern the volume of credit and currency needed by the country.
6.	The elimination of slumps and booms; and more direct procedure for eliminating unnecessary poverty.
7.	The abolition of the debt system where all credit is created by banks and hired out at interest to the country.
May I now revert for a time to the question of income tax? To show how widespread is
[Mr. Blackmore.l
the anxiety about income tax, and the demand for the reduction of it, may I refer to certain evidences which have appeared in Canada during the last two or three months? I turn to an article appearing in Saturday Night, the issue of March 8, 1947, under the title "Taxing the Wrong Thing". I quote:
It is beginning to be realized that the heavy taxation of income has the effect of destroying a great deal of the incentive to produce goods and services, and that, in the world's present situation, .that incentive needs to be left as effective as possible, because we certainly need all the goods and services which are currently being turned out, and a lot more.
Further down, under the heading "Killing Incentive", this passage appears:
It is production rather than consumptive demand that needs stimulating; and production is certainly not stimulated by a tax system which begins whittling away at the incentive to produce as soon as the annual income has reached $660. and reduces it practically to zero long before that income lias become really substantial. For the incentive to produce is simply the income which actually comes into the control of *the producer as a reward of his efforts. Money taken from the producer by the government has no incentive value; even if it is paid back to him by that government in welfare expenditures it is still no incentive, for he gets the benefit of those welfare expenditures, whether he produces or not.
I think I am safe in assuming that this organ speaks more or less for business, for what we might call capitalism.
Now may I turn to a periodical representing labour. I refer to the Canadian Unionist of April, 1947. Everyone in the house will recognize this paper as having a moderate, scientific and realistic approach to all matters of public concern. On page 76, column 2, I find an article entitled "Income Tax is Too High". I will not read the whole article; I merely' direct the attention of those interested to the beginning of paragraph 2 in which these words appear:
In its recent memorandum to the government, the congress called for a reduction of income taxes in order to provide exemptions for single persons earning $1,500 per year or less, and married persons earning $2,000 per year or less. Such an amendment is highly desirable because the income tax bears with a special severity upon workers with comparatively low incomes.
I think that is sufficient to represent labour. Much more could be referred to but I have no desire to use an undue amount of time.
And now I wish to refer to periodicals representing agriculture in Canada. Having done so I shall have cited expressions of opinion of the three main divisions of Canada's economy. In a periodical entitled "U.F.C. Information," of January 1947, I find an account of resolutions passed by the forty-

Prairie Farm Assistance Act
sixth central convention of the United Farmers of Canada. On page 5 we read the following resolution:
Whereas the present income tax exemption on single and married persons respectively is inadequate for a decent standard of living,
Therefore be it resolved that this convention demand that the income tax exemption be raised to $1,500 and $3,000 for single and married persons respectively, and
Furthermore be it resolved that the first $800 the farmer derives from the production of livestock and poultry be also exempt and the taxable income be spread over a five year period.
There is little doubt about the attitude of the people who passed that resolution. I turn now to page 11, where we have the minutes of district 4 convention, another group of farmers. At the bottom of the page I read as follows:
That this convention go on record as favouring an amendment to the Income Tax Act to allow for exemption of $1,500 for single status and $3,000 for married status.
I turn now to page 12 of the February 1947 issue and read the following statement at the close of an article called "Excerpts from a Farm Survey":
Another feature that was brought to our attention in answer to our question as to why they had changed to grain farming from mixed farming, was, ''Why should I work my head off raising cattle and feeding hogs and pay the greater part of the earnings in income tax?"
I think those are enough quotations and references to show clearly that my remarks about income tax are, in a broad way, representative of the people of Canada.
In closing I urge upon the minister that he forthwith bring in such modifications of the income tax regulations as will exempt all incomes of single persons of $1,500 and under and all incomes of married people of $3,000 and under.

speechtext:
There is a matter which I should like to bring to the attention of the house and through you, Mr. Speaker, to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in connection with the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. While this act has brought great benefits to the western provinces, I feel that it should now be submitted to a committee of the house with a view to having brought to the attention of the house certain recommendations for amendment of it. Members receive more correspondence on the Prairie Farm Assistance Act than on any other subject; and that can be understood when a short resume of the statistics is placed before the house.
The Prairie Farm Assistance Act has been in effect since 1939. Considerable areas in Saskatchewan and Alberta have been in receipt of payments under this act in seven out of the eight years during which it has been in effect. Recently a return was brought down in the house, sessional paper No. 7B of March 14, 1947, in answer to certain questions which I placed on the order paper. The questions asked were:
1.	What is the number of full townships in each of the prairie provinces which have received prairie farm assistance payments the following number of times: (a) 7: (b) 6: (e) 5; (d) 4; (e) 3; (f) 2; (g) 1?
2.	What was the total sum of payments received by each individual township and what was the total number of individual farmer payments in 1 (a)?
3.	What was the total acreage of cultivated land in 1946 on the farm which received prairie farm assistance in 1 (a) ?
The answers to these questions, which show the extent to which drought has affected crop conditions in the prairier provinces, are as follows:

Those statistics indicate the extent to which drought has affected large areas, not for one year but over a period of years, and the extent to which this act has been beneficial.
The act originally was passed in 1939 and there were amendments in 1940, chapter 38; in 1941, chapter 24; and in 1942, chapter 5. It was to be expected that in the operation of the act difficulties and anomalies would arise. In any event they are revealed only as a result of experience. The general objections which are raised to the act as it is at present constituted are as follows-and I suggest that these objections be placed before a committee representative of the western farmers, to the end that the act may be amended in accordance with the results of its operation.
First, it is contended that payment should be on the basis of the individual farmer. Whether or not that be so, I think there should be some change so that at least a por-

Prairie Farm. Assistance Act

t-ion of a township, even though not contiguous to another township, might come within the terms of the act.
Second, the act should be broadened so as to include some payment for hail damage, on an individual basis. The minister in his reply may say that insurance can be had against that risk.

speechtext: They pay on hail now.

speechtext:
Yes. The point I make is that so far as hail is concerned it should be applicable on an individual basis. The objection ordinarily raised to placing the whole act on an individual basis certainly does not apply to hail damage. If all payments were placed upon an individual basis, the argument might be advanced that a premium was being placed upon indifferent farming, or farming on submarginal lands. That argument is not applicable so far as hail damage is concerned.
The third point is that present payments are insufficient. They are beneficial so far as they go. They could not be expected to go as far as a system of crop insurance. But the general feeling expressed by farmers in western Canada is that, if the act were revamped and certain changes made, they would have no objection to an increase in the amount now deducted from their production.
The next objection is that the act discriminates against larger farmers. While I realize that a certain unit must be established, nevertheless I feel that the maximum amount payable should be increased, and that that maximum should be fixed at least at the sum of $1,000.
There is considerable criticism of the regulation which provides that an applicant, to be entitled under the act, is required to live on his land, or at least to devote himself solely to agriculture. Numbers of farmers over the years have paid the one per cent deduction compulsorily, yet from year to year they have been denied any return, irrespective of whether or not they have suffered drought damage. Some change should be made in the act whereby a man who operates his business in conjunction with another business should not be denied payment under the act.
I shall now refer specifically to two cases, although the four or five points to which I

have directed attention are discussed generally by farmers throughout the west. I wish to bring to the attention of the house two examples in support of my argument that a change in the act is necessary.
One has to do with the rural municipality of Dufferin, in Saskatchewan. Year by year a portion of that municipality, by reason of a valley which runs alongside of it, must suffer continuing drought; yet because it is not contiguous to a municipality declared eligible under the act, the farmers there resident are denied any consideration. From year to year contributions are made; from year to year the contributors are denied any return. While I am familiar with the difficulty of changing the act in order to meet individual cases, only a small amendment will be necessary to bring this and a number of similar cases within the provisions. After all, the purpose of the act is to ensure that a farmer shall not be denied some return from a crop which he had expected but which was destroyed by drought or some other climatic condition.
I should like to refer to another case in support of my argument that the act should be amended so as to provide for the inclusion of a portion of a township, if the individual basis already suggested be not accepted. This has to do with the rural municipality of Craik, but one of many. Here certain farmers in an area not contiguous to a township eligible under the act, find themselves denied any payment. The suggestion comes from the council of the municipality, and states that the farmers generally would favour the necessity of providing for the placing of townships, if necessary, within the system. It states:
At present the provisions are too rigid to do other than make for great unfairness in practically all partial township considerations.
And then the secretary treasurer of this municipality says:
It is an absolute miscarriage of the basic underlying principle of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act if they in great need, do not get the bonus when their neighbours immediately south do get same because their area extends two miles further east to the boundary of the township.
The general attitude of rural municipal-officials throughout western Canada is summed up in this letter, a copy of which I understand was sent to the minister, and which states:
In whole the act needs a spring-cleaning and the human equation, which is the equation aimed to be aided, given consideration instead of the present equation of townships and blocks being the factor in main consideration to the detriment of many human beings-
-who should be qualified.

Immigration
I am suggesting the minister should give consideration to changing the act. Hon. members representing constituencies from the three western provinces have all had experience with its operation, and would all be in a position to make suggestions to the government. In order to cover situations such as I have mentioned, which cause an injustice and certainly develop a feeling of resentment on the part of those who are disqualified because of the rigidity of the act as it now stands, the act should be amended. I am asking the minister if he will give hon. members an opportunity to place before the committee on agriculture the changes which they believe to be necessary. I understand of course that the adoption of those recommendations would remain a matter of government policy, but I think an opportunity should be given hon. members to express their views and to place before the government the picture of conditions prevailing under the act. I believe their recommendations would be beneficial not only to the government but to the country as a whole.

IMMIGRATION-DISPLACED PERSONS AND REFUGEES-DOMESTIC AND OTHER WORKERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish first of all to associate myself with the remarks of the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) in connection with the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. What he has advocated today is substantially the same as my colleagues from Saskatchewan and I urged last year in the discussion on the estimates of the Department of Agriculture.
Perhaps I will be pardoned if I now leave that subject in order to bring to the attention of the house and the country a matter which seems to me to be one of urgency and of considerable public interest and concern. I refer to the question of immigration. From time to time we have had debates in this house referring in part to immigration. We have had several statements from the government side on various phases of immigration, but I do not think it would be overdrawing it to say that there is a great deal of confusion and bewilderment in the minds of the people as to the exact policy of the government on immigration.
The particular phase of immigration which I want to emphasize today is not the general or long-term policy, which I understand is still in the making, but the immediate and urgent question of what is to be done so far as we in Canada are concerned about the displaced persons and refugees now in Europe. This question is not new in the house, and 83166-1584
unfortunately it is not new in Europe. The matter is becoming more urgent every hour.
The action we have had in the past has been, to say the least, disappointing to the public mind. On August 13, 1946, a committee of the senate which was dealing with immigration and labour presented its report, and I should like to quote from page 311, as follows:
Immigrants who come to Canada on the responsibility of relatives or friends already here enjoy a real advantage over those who arrive as complete strangers. The right to bring relatives and friends here is a privilege which our government may well extend to Canadian citizens.
Then further down reference is made to order in council 2071 passed on May 28, 1946, as follows:
The order in council has meant nothing to date, for practically no immigrants are being admitted, whether relatives or otherwise, nor are any steps being taken with a view to future admission.
That was August 13, 1946, and we are now well into 1947. That last statement seems to be substantially true today. The Minister of Mines and Resources- (Mr. Glen) has stated in this house on several occasions that the regulations dealing with the admissible classes of prospective immigrants are being widened and relaxed.

maintopic: IMMIGRATION-DISPLACED PERSONS AND REFUGEES-DOMESTIC AND OTHER WORKERS
speechtext:
I was about to say that the action taken so far in connection with bringing into Canada relatives and friends of those already resident in Canada has been disappointing, and that the lack of action which was indicated in August, 1946, seems to continue. A delegation interviewed the government on February 7 of this year, and in order to indicate that there was a lack of 
action in connection with this particular phase of immigration I should like to quote from a pamphlet entitled "The Refugee" which reports the visit of this delegation. One of the things mentioned in their brief was this:
The plight of at least 800,000 refugees, displaced persons and orphans is so desperate that quick action is necessary if any considerable numbers are to obtain a haven of refuge in Canada. So we respectfully plead for immediate action on our request.
I am not attempting to go into all the ramifications of the government policy; I simply am trying to urge upon the government that the time has come when something substantial will have to be done about this question of refugees and displaced persons. I should like to point out that the delegation to which I have just referred represented a large number of people. For example, the following organizations were represented:
Ukrainian Canadian committee.
Ukrainian Canadian veterans association.
Canadians citizens of Polish origin.
Mennonite board of colonization.
Lutheran world relief.
Committee for the relief of democratic refugees.
Monsignor Basil Markle, representing Most Reverend P. J. Monahan in the name of the Catholic bishops of the prairie provinces, and Catholic immigration aid society.
Those organizations represent hundreds of thousands of people in Canada. All they were asking the government to do was to take action as quickly as possible in permitting persons for whom applications had already been made, or were being made, to enter this country at the earliest opportunity.
We were disturbed to find that recently the government has been following a new sort of immigration line in allowing certain industries to bring in workers under contract as cheap labour. I hope that is not the type of policy that is to be followed as an alternative to bringing into Canada the relatives and friends of persons resident here. The senate committee definitely recommended in favour of the policy of giving priority to persons who w'ould be received here by friends and relatives and be given a start in the Canadian way of life in preference to the bringing in of cheap labour.
When I speak of displaced persons or refugees I want to make myself clear so that there will be no misunderstanding of what I mean. I shall quote from the constitution of the International Refugee Organization the definition of a displaced person and the conditions under which such persons should be given refuge in other countries. In this same booklet from which I have been quoting

Immigration
refugees are described as persons who objected to returning to their former countries of residence because of-
,(i) persecution, or fear, based on reasonable grounds or persecution because of race, religion, nationality or political opinions, provided these opinions are not in conflict with the principles of the united nations, as laid down in the preamble of the charter of the united nations
In other words, persons who find themselves in displaced persons camps in Europe for one reason or another and who have no criminal record or anything which would disqualify them from becoming good and respectable citizens. I believe that the majority of the members of this house would agree that such people would make desirable citizens for Canada.
What is to be the policy of the government? We have heard on several occasions from the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) of one type of immigration policy. For example on April 25, on Friday last, he was referring to the bringing into Canada of labour for the sugar beet farms and for a textile mill in Quebec. I quote from Hansard:
Mr. Mitchell: If I can say this to my hon. friend-
He was interrupted and then he went on:
Mr. Mitchell: -just a minute now; we have had speeches on both sides of the house advocating immigration, and as soon as we set the policy in motion, you understand, there is a slight reservation on the part of some hon. gentlemen.
What intrigued me was his remark "as soon as we set the policy in motion." To what policy was he referring? If the government has already decided on a policy it is something the members of the house do not know about, because the house has not yet been taken into the confidence of the government and told what its immigration policy is.
We also had the experience of reading in the press that the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Hartt) who was then a candidate in the by-election, had announced the government's immigration policy in the course of that by-election. That announcement was later denied by the minister responsible for immigration. All these different announcements and denials and different steps being taken have created a feeling of confusion and bewilderment in the minds of the people, who are hoping for quick action in connection with their applications for the admission of relatives and friends.
May I add this for the benefit of the minister of immigration, that even if there is not transportation available for those persons on whose behalf application has already been made for their admission to Canada, I feel
that the government should take steps to issue visas to those who are within the admissible classes and who would make desirable citizens, so that they will have something tangible to show that they are to be given an opportunity eventually to come to this country. The worst feature of the whole situation in Europe is that these persons who have been in displaced persons camps some for two years, and some for much longer, are deteriorating in morale-I do not think that is too strong a statement-because they do not know what is going to happen to them. They cannot say for certain that they will be allowed to come to Canada or to one of the other western democracies, and they do not know that they will not be forced to return to their country of origin or what will happen to them. Every day that we procrastinate and delay, their morale and their usefulness further decreases, and they will make that much less desirable citizens for Canada. The government might well consider the issuing of visas in advance to persons in these displaced persons camps who are found to be in the admissible classes, so that they will have something to live for, some ray of hope that at some future day when transportation is available they can come to Canada.
I want to refer to a recommendation made by the delegation which interviewed the government on February 7 in connection with the regulations governing "relatives". Under the regulations the term "relatives" is very restricted in its meaning. The delegation recommended that a change be made in P.C. 2071 and P.C. 371/47, to include all the immediate relatives of any persons legally admitted and resident in Canada who are in a position to receive and care for such relatives. By immediate relatives they mean "up to and including first cousins and their children".
I would also refer to a meeting held in Toronto earlier this year at which the hon. member for Trinity (Mr. Skey) and I were present at which fifteen hundred people passed a resolution dealing with this same question, advocating the widening of the regulations to include all immediate relatives rather than just some restricted classes. There is a good reason for that, because often it is found that if the present regulations were to be followed strictly there would have to be a division of families. In some cases the father might be allowed in to the country but other members of his family might be barred. This works a hardship and an injustice on people who have already suffered more than their share of hardship and injustice.
I hope that the minister will find it possible to announce to the house today the specific
Immigration

things which the government has in mind in connection with admitting displaced persons and refugees say within the next six months. We have been told again and again that transportation is not available and other things are not as they should be. That is possibly quite true. But if we look at it from the point of view of humanity and realize that we are not dealing with a cargo of dry goods which can stand waiting on the European shore for the next three or four years, we shall realize that our immigration policy is a question of real urgency. Surely transportation and shipping can be made available if this country desires that it should be made available at this time.

maintopic: IMMIGRATION-DISPLACED PERSONS AND REFUGEES-DOMESTIC AND OTHER WORKERS
speechtext:
Before the house resolves itself into committee of supply, I wish to complain about the great scarcity of ships for bringing people out from the old country. I have been in touch with some of the shipping companies and have been told that shipping is practically sold out for the next year, with the result, as the hon. member said a moment ago, very little can be done about securing shipping.
I object to the government bringing out Polish soldiers'. As was said in the British House of Commons, they were not all conscripted'; most of them were volunteers. They were told that if they enlisted on the side of Germany they would have food and clothing and might not have to fight. They obtained better conditions than if they had stayed at home and done their duty as good citizens of a great Polish country. I object inasmuch as the British government is paying the fares of these people to bring them out. As was announced in the house last week, a team from this country has gone over there to prepare the way for these people to come to Canada. We were not told what parts of this country they were to come to. At the same time we find that it is difficult for citizens of the old country to get to Canada because there is no shipping space.
I object to the government bringing out these people because in Italy they were fighting against the British forces and against our own forces. That was shown in the British House of Commons. Shipping space can be found for these people, but for the British, who bore the heat and burden of the day during the war, no shipping space can be found.
I have had a lot of correspondence with one shipping company which has ships on the seven seas, and they tell me that shipping space has been sold out for almost a year. There will not be anything available until the

fall and there may not be anything then. Charity should begin at home. We should think of these people, our own kith and kin, who protected our shores against invasion during the difficult days of the war.
I was surprised at the reply which has been given us here by the government regarding these Polish soldiers and others, because the real facts are set out in a return which has been tabled in parliament in the old country. Objection has been taken to that policy here. A large number of these men fought against us in Italy and in other parts of Europe. They were not all conscripted; a large majority of them were volunteers. They gave up their Polish citizenship, and when the Germans came through their country they welcomed the Germans with open arms and tried to get into the German army.
Perhaps we should not do everything that the British government asks. They pay the fares of these men. God help this country if we have to depend on everything that the present Labour government is doing at the present time in the old country. They are stifling private initiative and private enterprise. They have made a mess of their internal situation with regard to coal, floods, food and electric power, and their foreign affairs. They are giving away and scattering parts of the empire for a song. We hope that there will not be such a state of affairs in Canada.
I object to the policy of the government regarding shipping and its immigration policy. It is well known that hardly anybody from the old country can come to this country; they cannot get shipping, or comply with the immigration regulations. Conditions are not what they should be. The result is that most of these British people are going to New Zealand and Australia, particularly the soldiers who fought for the country. They did something for the dominions and for the old country. Instead of sending a large delegation to Lake Success-it should be called Lake Failure or Lake Farce-to look into the Palestine problem which will be nothing but tower of babel; we should give some consideration to immigration from the old country. The same thing applies to the united nations. It is nothing but a tower of babel. What useful purpose will be served by inquiring into conditions in Palestine when we know as has been charged in the British House of Commons, that wealthy Jews of New York city and other parts of the United States are the people who are supplying the money to bring these bandit, illegal, underground gangsters into Palestine. This charge has been made by the opposition in

Immigration
the old country. Wealthy people of the United States belonging to one race are financing what is going on in Palestine. These terrorists are murdering in cold blood officers of the Eighth army and others. In the face of that we are sending delegates to Lake Success to inquire into the Palestine situation, with which we have no connection whatever. We should release shipping to bring immigrants from Great Britain. A large number of ships were leased to us by the United States government during the war. I hope the head of the government, who has charge of this, will take up these matters to see if some shipping cannot be provided during the next two or three months for our kith and kin in the old country, and not leave it until it is too late.
From the information I have received from shipping companies, it is clear that shipping space has been all sold for the next year. The practical result is that people who want to come out here with their families or brothers or sisters, fathers and mothers are not able to do so. Some want to go to the prairies, and some want to go to other parts of the country to be with their kith and kin. I do hope that the government will take the matter up and that we shall have some reply, because I do not want to see all the people in the mother country who served in our forces have to go to New Zealand and Australia. That is where they are going. The minister did some good work. He opened some shipping immigration agencies in Belfast and Liverpool. We had one in London and in Glasgow one was opened. Tens of thousands of people want to come to this country but they cannot get the shipping space. Surely the government must have some ships. Then there are the private companies, the merchant marine and other ships which could be utilized by lease or charter parties to give us space for the next six months, so that people of the mother country could migrate here instead of having to go to New Zealand and Australia.

maintopic: IMMIGRATION-DISPLACED PERSONS AND REFUGEES-DOMESTIC AND OTHER WORKERS
speechtext:
I wish to raise the question of the treatment of women workers being admitted to Canada to work in the textile mills and in domestic employment. We are all alarmed at the trend that government policy has taken. AVe have been told for the last two or three years, and during the three sessions since I have been a member, that the government had a policy and that under that policy certain people could be admitted; but we found that it was a restricted policy. It applied only to the immediate relatives of persons who were
already in Canada. When we tried to get in cousins, uncles or inlaws, we were denied the right to bring them in. Now we find that the industrialists of this country are being given permission to set our immigration policy, because in effect that is how it is working out. If someone wants so many workers, by order in council he is given the right to go and bring in so many hundred people. I for one object to having any section of our economy set the immigration policy of this government. I think I voice the sentiments of every hon. member in that regard. If we are to bring people in by the hundreds and allow others to add to that number we should consider the field of immigration as a whole.
AVe should remember that the whole question of retaining population in Canada itself is an important one. In the thirty years preceding the war, between 1901 and 1931, our record was not very good in that respect. We find that in those thirty years the natural increase was three and a half million. In the same thirty years we brought in 5,100,000 people. So that our total population should have grown by eight and a half million people. But at the end of thirty years our population was not up to the extent of eight and a half million people. The real increase was only five million people. Therefore we had lost three and a half million people during the time we were bringing in 5,100,000 immigrants. When you break down that figure you find that, of the 3,500,000 people who left Canada,
1.000.000 were Canadian born and 2,500,000 went somewhere else, or asked to be sent back to their own country. This included many British people who applied for repatriation during the depression. This total meant that half of our immigrants moved on and a million of our own people who moved out.
I submit that this is a serious condition. We find that not only do our own people move out, but the people who are most expensive to train leave us. Our scientists, teachers and medical men move out. I have here the review of Canadian Health Needs and Health Insurance Proposals, which tells us that while no precise figures are available, a national health survey estimated that the loss in immigration is the equivalent of not less than ten per cent of our medical school output. In other words, ten per cent of our young doctors move out, so that we are losing the most highly trained and valuable people at the top, while we are recruiting people to come in on the lowest occupational level. [DOT]
Let me assure the house that I am not against bringing in either immigrants or

__________ Immigration
refugees, but we must separate the two, because we have a definite responsibility, which we have shirked, in regard to the need of displaced persons to find refuge in sanctuary. We have been very selfish, for many people must have died because we refused to take seriously our responsibility in this regard. The question of displaced persons and refugees must not, however, be confused with the problem of immigration, and our industrialists must not be permitted to determine our immigration policy through an operational move out the back door. That is what I object to.
In connection with refusals, I suggest that there are many worthy cases that are being denied all the time. I have here a letter with reference to a Norwegian who escaped from Norway and joined the merchant marine of the resistance forces. He was in the British command and shipped in and out of Canadian ports all through the war. He came to Little Norway and became engaged to a Canadian girl. This man is young and healthy, earning his own living, and is engaged to a Canadian, having been in the Canadian merchant marine, but he is now told that he cannot come to Canada. Just last week I saw a letter from the Immigration branch telling him that he could not come here, but an industrialist can get permission to bring in 100 or 500 textile workers from somewhere else.
That is what we must object to as members of parliament, the denial of our responsibility to persons who have already proved themselves worthy of admittance, while we grant a permit to someone to go and drag in so many hundred people to fill a textile mill.
In regard to this particular question, I wish to talk about the status of those women who will be brought to work in the province of Quebec. So far as the move to bring in workers is concerned, I think it is unfortunate that the order in council dealing with textile workers, which I have before me, and which permits their entry under the auspices of the Dionne Spinning Mill Company, is framed in the way in which it is. There is an application for admittance from Europe of 100 women for training and employment as .textile workers, and they are to be paid at wages as required by the law of Quebec regulating salaries and conditions of work in the textile industry of that province.
As members we must bear in mind that the textile industry is one of the most poorly paid in Canada. I have that on the authority of the year book for 1946 which gives the wages paid in every industry and the average wages for each province. I find that the maritimes and Quebec are the worst employers and 
have the worst wages; and of all the industries, the textile is one of the very worst in the matter of wages. It is therefore unfortunate that we should bring these women in and put them in the worst industry in the worst province. If we are to do that we should give them at least as much protection as we give the Polish veterans. The Polish veterans who are being brought in under the national employment office contract will have exactly the same treatment wherever they go in Canada- the same wages, the same contract. The Polish veteran will not be the victim of any one province or the victim of any low-paid industry. The government is to be complimented on working out a national agreement with the Polish veterans, but I would ask it to do the same for the women workers who come in to take employment in Canada. If we are to bring in men and women we must give them equal protection under the laws of the country.
I wish to discuss now the question of the domestic worker, which is of interest to everyone, because, according to the James report on reconstruction, the home is a valuable institution. I do not think any of us have any quarrel with that. We all agree that help for the mother in the home is necessary. Here is a paragraph that all hon. members should be interested in. I think it is relevant:
In any measure of social policy in which regard is had to fact, the great majority of married women must be regarded as occupied in work which is vital though unpaid, without which their husbands could not do the paid work and without which the nation could not continue.
If we are to bring in people to work in our homes we must have regard for the homes in which they will serve. I think it is regrettable, but it has been accepted that the stupid people who could not get work in anything else could always do housework and could look after children, and we have paid them accordingly. That stigma which we have put upon housework has made it almost impossible to get girls to work in homes now that there is work to be had in other industries.
I have here a table from the 1941 census which shows how poorly paid the domestic worker has been, although the domestic worker has had an important part to play in the question as to the number of women who work in domestic employment in comparison with the number of teachers, office workers and others. Office workers are only five per cent of the women workers, teachers only eleven per cent, whereas the women who did housework in 1941 constituted 24 per cent of all women workers. So that from the point of view of numbers they are important, because they are more than twice as numerous

as the teachers and five times as numerous as the office workers. But here are the wages they were paid in cash, and many of them did not get board and lodging. Charwomen, cleaners and cooks did not get board and lodging in many cases. Cleaners and charwomen get an average of S358 a year; cooks get an average of $447 a year; housekeepers and matrons range from $235 to $364 a year; and in the domestic and allied trades the wages were from $285 to $366, according to the dominion bureau of statistics, 1941 census.

speechtext:
If we are to bring women in we should inquire whether or not there are openings in this field. Last Tuesday I attended, in the railway committee room in this building, a meeting which was called by the Department of Labour and attended by the mayor of this city and representatives of all the national women's organizations. We were told that there were 2,700 women looking for work and that there were between 400 and 500 positions open to them. So that does not indicate to me that in Ottawa at least there is any great shortage of domestic help. But the conditions of employment and the social status that goes with domestic employment have, I think, made women and girls reluctant to enter this field.
The government has a responsibility to the homes of this country, to the mothers and to the women who would do that kind of work if it were put on the basis of a profession and were paid decently. The recommendations of this commission are useful as a guide to the government in undertaking that sort of thing. This report recommends that training schools for domestic workers be set up. If the government is to admit girls from Europe, this is especially important, although it is also important from the point of view of our untrained workers here or the people who should be doing domestic work. This suggestion of a training programme is a sensible and useful one. The recommendation is that the training be part time and that, while the girl is training, she work part time. That is, the girl would go to school perhaps in the morning and would work in the afternoon.
She would also earn at the same time as she was training, and there would be less of a load as far as the expense of conducting these schools is concerned; she would gain selfrespect and she would immediately begin to realize that her work would be useful, necessary and worth while.
The government should consider carefully this suggestion made by women who are representative of women's organizations, and I think there are national women's organizations which would be only too happy to assist the Department of Labour in setting up these schools. I am sure that the Young Women's Christian Association and the National Council of Women would help. These women were at the meeting last week; they are to have a meeting tomorrow in the same place, and they are anxious that we raise the standards not only of the workers, but of the women who employ them, because the women who employ them have been guilty of a faulty attitude in regard to their employees. I see no reason why these girls should not have hostels. Many of them are not going to be able to live in. The modern house is small. The modern apartment is cramped and there is not room to house the worker. In addition to that, the worker herself -would much rather have living accommodation outside the home of her employer. As I mentioned last week at the meeting where we discussed this matter, I think the day is past when the maid should be relegated to the attic and be given the use of all the cast-off furniture. If this is to be a respectable and respected occupation, the girl has a right to a nice room in an attractive hostel and should be paid enough so that she could pay for her room on a reasonable basis. This was the approach which the people in New Zealand were using when I was there a few years ago. They were experiencing an industrial boom, and they found that their girls were very happy to flock out of the homes and into the factories, although many of them would have preferred to do housework. Therefore the people of that country were establishing minimum wages and hours legislation and were building hostels, so that the girls could have a social life of their own among people who were in a like occupation. That was a great improvement on the original status of the household employee.
I am going to ask the government that, if we are to bring in women, we do two things. I ask that the industrial worker coming from Europe be given the same protection as the Polish veteran, under a national labour code and contract; and that household workers, if we bring in household workers, be given the advan-

Immigration

tage of training and the advantage of protection by law. I urge that, because we still have many people in Canada who believe that to be different is to be inferior and who will treat these people as inferior persons because they speak a different language, have a different kind of dress, and are not accustomed to eat the same kind of food. It is a common fallacy1, one into which all of us easily drop, to look on people who are different as not being as good as we are, and to treat them accordingly. We must not permit that to happen. I am going to ask the government to see to it that we give this protection to our women immigrants.

Mr. Speaker, I feel I should say a word or two about immigration, seeing that you have permitted a few members to speak previously this afternoon on that matter. A number of my constituents have written to me about immigration and they are concerned about the government's policy. I want to say that I and those who support me are in favour of admitting to this country as many as possible of those people who fought for us or were on our side or who have our ideals. I think we have to do the best we can for refugees in Europe and other countries.
I want, in a few words, to express opposition to certain things. The first matter I should like to mention is the bringing into this country of former members of the second Polish corps. I think the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) has said that this was one of the finest immigration schemes that had ever been evolved in Canada, but when there are so many people in dire need wishing to come to this country I do not think there is any necessity of bringing in any more of these soldiers under the present terms. I have here a paper called The Commonwealth of April 25, 1947. This is a leading Catholic weekly, and I should like to quote as follows:
Cardinal Sapieha has recently appealed to Poles abroad to return to Poland, assuring them that all who have not lost their citizenship can return without fear. . . .
I am sure that, in view of a statement like that being made by such high authority, large numbers of these men will want to leave England and other points for Poland. I have no doubt that among the former Polish soldiers who were admitted there are many splendid men, many democrats, but in my opinion there are others who are not. I understand that we have brought in something in the neighbourhood of 150 who formerly served in the German army. I want to express my opposition to that. There are so many hundreds of thousands of people who are unquestionably suitable immigrants and, when that is so, I do not think we should bring to this country anyone who has rendered service in the German armed forces during the last war.
I wish to speak briefly with reference to the Ukrainians. I know there are thousands of democratic Ukrainians who wish to come to this country, and I would be one who would welcome all who are thoroughly democratic in their outlook. But we must not forget that there were four divisions of 83166-159J
Ukrainians who fought as volunteers in the German army, and we must be very careful that we do not let any of those birds into this country. When it comes to a question of selection I am sure that when our officers come to examine these people they will find that they all claim they are democrats.
In addition, I want to express my opposition, as did the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mrs. Strum), to the bringing in of contract labour under the circumstances under which they are apparently being brought in to work in the textile mills. I have had a number of letters in that connection and I am quite sure that will be a most unpopular procedure with Canadian labour throughout Canada.
I know it is very easy to talk on this subject. Immigration is a difficult question and I admit the difficulties. I am of opinion that if this government is to work out an immigration policy which will find general acceptance in this country it can do so only on the basis of having discussions with leaders of the veterans organizations, labour organizations and farm organizations. If the government is willing to do that and get their varying points of view I believe it will find that there is a measure of common agreement among them and that an immigration policy can be worked out which would be satisfactory to and supported by a large majority of the Canadian people, one which would at the same time assist great numbers of these refugees and other worthy people who wish to come to this country from Europe.

Then, I cannot put a question on the order paper in respect of it because it is a matter dealing with the house itself. I have been at a loss, therefore, to know when to bring it up, and I appreciate the opportunity afforded this afternoon.
The matter I have in mind' is in respect of a revision of parliamentary procedure, something which I suggest is long overdue. We have come to a stage in our governmental and parliamentary history when we have become something more than legislators, and when governments, through the very nature of our nation's business, find that parliamentary sessions are lasting longer and longer. It is in this connection I have one or two suggestions to make.
In the last two years special committees have been appointed to make some few recommendations in respect of house pro-

cedure. I was a member of the committee last year, and we sat just once. For some unknown reason-at least unknown to me-we did not meet again. There seems to be some sort of influence radiating from some place or another which defeats our progress in the matter of revising our rules of procedure. This year no committee has been set up.
I am not going to take up the time of the house this afternoon to go into all the ramifications and regulations as to what procedure could be revised, but I have a suggestion to make, one which has been made before, but about which nothing has been done. We make it again; and if we have to make it again we will keep on making it, until something is done. The suggestion is that much time could be saved in the house if, through common consent, hon. members would permit the estimates to go before the various parliamentary committees, there to be discussed and from there to be brought back to the house for final vote.

For instance, there is the Department of Fisheries. There are very few things in that department which might interest my constituents, but there is an afternoon's discussion on lobster traps. My goodness, I have not any lobsters in my constituency; I am not interested in that, and yet I have to be here. There is one other matter I should like to deal with, a matter which I think is being considered favourably by a good many members. I refer to the hours of our sittings. I do not know whether hon. members find what I do; but, as the months go by, I find it rather a grind to get to my office at ten o'clock in the morning and stay here until eleven o'clock at night. That is a pretty good sized day. By the time I get to my sleeping quarters, which is not my home, and do the one or two things I have to do before retiring, such as brushing my teeth, I find that it is about one o'clock before I can turn in. I am quite confident that hon. members would find their work much more pleasant if the hours of sitting were rearranged.
I suppose a dozen different suggestions could be made respecting change in hours, but I am going to suggest that we do not sit on Monday nights, on Wednesday nights or on Friday nights and that the hours in the afternoon be from two o'clock until six o'clock. That works out to just one hour less per week than what we are putting in now. It would mean that the only nights we would sit would be on Tuesdays and Thursdays. I do not see how the cabinet ministers stand the grind of attending to their departmental work, being responsible for their own legislation and seeing to the administration of their departments. When their estimates are up they have to sit here until eleven o'clock at night and they have as much responsibility for being here as any other hon. member. I do not know how the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) stands the grind. Perhaps he goes home in the evening and I am quite willing that he should because he has a tremendous responsibility, but there are some others who would like to go home in the evening as well. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is an entirely different matter that I should like to speak on for a few minutes. I address my remarks in particular to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie). On April 23 I directed a question to the minister as to whether consideration was being given by the government to amending the War Veterans Allowance Act to provide an increase in the amount of the allowance both for veterans and for the widows of non-pensioned veterans. The minister made a forthright reply, and I appreciate the fact that he gave a clear-cut answer to my question. He said, as reported at page 2332 of Hansard:
It is not the intention of the government to introduce at the present session of parliament any amendments to the War Veterans' Allowance Act.
The grievance that I raise is to protest against that decision and to make an appeal to the minister and to the government to reconsider the matter at an early date. I do so in particular on behalf of non-pensioned veterans' widows.
As hon. members know, the dominion council of the organization representing these widows was in Ottawa last week. Most members are familiar-the matter is fresh in our minds at the present time and that is why I raise it now-with the situation in which these women find themselves. It is true that in recent years the government has taken certain steps in favour of these widows by establishing a special allowance for them. But-particularly with rising prices, the effect of which is being recognized in that the old age pension is to be raised-these widows feel that the time has come for the government to give consideration to their request for an increase in the amount. They now receive a maximum of $30.41 a month. The amount they are asking for is the modest sum of $40 a month. There are a number of other requests but I shall name just two of them. The second request is the matter of providing for hospitalization for these wddows when they require it. The third matter is that of making this allowance available to widows of all non-pensioned veterans of the South African war and the first world war rather than to the restricted group which is now the case because of the definition of an actual

theatre of war. That is all one needs to say on the point at this moment, for surely it is not necessary to emphasize the plight of these women in view of the meagre amount that they now receive.
As I say, the minister has made a definite statement as to the intention of the government this year, but I do make a plea to him to reconsider the matter and see if the government cannot, before the session is over, either in the estimates or in some other way, improve the position of these deserving widows of Canada's non-pensioned veterans.
