ALLOWANCES TO DISABLED VETERANS ATTENDING UNIVERSITY
speechtext:
There is one matter I wish to bring to the attention of the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie). When a veteran goes to the university, if he is single he gets an allowance of $60 a month. If a veteran goes to Osgoode Hall he is allowed to make $40 as well, which brings his amount up to $100. If a veteran receives a pension of $50 a month, all that he receives in the form of an allowance is $10. I have in mind a veteran who is a disability case, and all that he is getting from the government in the way of an allowance is $10. Of course he has his pension, but he is not in as good a position as the other chap at Osgoode Hall who is able to make $40 in addition to his allowance of $60. The chap to whom I refer also goes to Osgoode Hall, but because he has lost a leg he is not able to make $40 a month. It seems to me a great pity that a man who has a disability should suffer the loss of part of his allowance. This allowance should be given to him as of right and he should have his pension free. It is much more difficult for the chap who is pensioned to get along and make a few dollars than for the other fellow. It does not seem right that the allowance which he gets for his education should be deducted if he receives a pension.
I have received several letters along the same lines from these chaps, and I think something should be done about the matter, because there is a grave injustice if this is the case. It is particularly hard on a lad who is going to university when he is suffering from a disability of any kind, because he cannot get around in the same way as the others. It is a pity that he should be penalized and his pension taken from him when that pension is for a definite purpose. If a man goes out and makes $60 or $100 a month you do not cut out his pension because he is earning money. Suppose he makes only $50; you do not deduct the pension from the amount of money he makes. Why should you deduct the amount of his pension from his allowance? I suggest that his pension is something that should be considered apart from any allowance he receives. I wish the minister would look into this matter.
I should like to endorse what the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said in regard to the widows. Some of these women are older now and they need all the money they can get. It seems to me that $30 a month is a pretty small allowance for them.

Daylight Saving Time

I wish to register a mild protest against daylight saving, which came into effect this morning. I wondered what was wrong when the maid rapped at my door at the unusual hour she did. I had to alter the clock and get up an hour earlier. I make this complaint not for myself, because I have enjoyed daylight saving. When I was younger it was harder for me to get up an hour earlier; but I find, as age is creeping up on me, it is no bother for me to get up at any time in the morning. I am speaking for the rural people, the farmers particularly. They are definitely opposed to the adoption of daylight saving piecemeal as we have it at present. When the war was at its height and daylight saving was standardized throughout Canada we got used to it; we worked by it and it was all right. Now that the decision has been left to the individual municipality, the situation is different. In the town in which I live they have adopted daylight saving to the detriment of the rural people, upon whom they depend for their prosperity. I was at a municipal gathering not so long ago where the officials of every municipality in the county were gathered and they definitely passed a resolution opposing daylight saving.
I do not know whether this matter comes under dominion jurisdiction, but I suggest that if we are to have the new time it should be in effect throughout Canada. We ought to have some heart for the rural people. Here it is, almost the first of May. The weather is cold; the farmer has seeding to do; he will be working his head off-I had almost said his fool head, because that is pretty nearly what it will mean'-in order to raise crops to feed a hungry world, and we are making it harder for him by adopting daylight saving time.
The farmer has to get casual labour from the urban municipality and quitting time comes at five or six o'clock, so that his hired help leaves him at the very time when, as those of us who have been brought up on farms know, the farmer is most in need of assistance. When the afternoon sun is shining, and toward evening, then the farmer needs all the help he can get. Once more I protest on behalf of Lambton-Kent, where I live, against the adoption of daylight saving. I protest on behalf of the rural people.

All Canada was shocked to learn of the tragedy that struck my constituency of Pontiac in the accident at the Malartic mine. We had all
hoped that the eleven men trapped in the mine would be rescued, but the latest news has dashed our hopes. It now appears that eleven families are bereaved. I wish at this time to express my sorrow at the accident and my sympathy with these stricken families. At the same time I would call the attention of the Canadian people to the necessity for greater vigilance and a more rigid enforcement of safety regulations in the mines of Canada, so that tragedies of the kind at Malartic may be of less frequent occurrence in the future.

Every hon. member will undoubtedly agree with the remarks of the hon. member for Pontiac and join him in the expression of sympathy to the bereaved.
I wish to associate myself, Mr. Speaker, with *what the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) has said and I hope the minister will give seridus consideration in the reasonable request that has been made by the women's delegation. I should like to say to the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that I agree with his sentiments in behalf of the women.

The matter I wish to raise is really a grievance of some urgency at this time, because the prospect or the possibility of discussing it under a specific order will likely be some days or maybe weeks away; I do not know when the opportunity will come. It is in the matter of a ruling of the Department of National Eev-enue in its application to the taxation of cooperative associations. The recent ruling has been that cooperative associations, when making up their accounts and the allocation of dividends for the year, must differentiate between those which are paid for provident purposes and those which are paid for productive purposes.
The patron of a cooperative association who receives a dividend on consumer or household goods that he has bought, does not have that apply to his income for taxation. But a dividend on what he buys for productive purposes -that is in the field of gasoline or those things for power work and so on-becomes part of his income and is taxable. Whether there is much quarrel with that particular division is a matter of opinion, but I should like to draw to the attention of the minister concerned that it is practically impossible for the cooperative associations to carry out that ruling. For instance, suppose a farmer comes in to buy some lumber from a cooperative that handles lumber. He takes away his truckload of

Another part might be used for some little repairs or patchwork on the steps leading into the house, the porch, or something of that kind. The same thing applies with regard to gasoline. Much of the gasoline may go into the tractor, or it may go into the car when the car is being used for the operation of the farm. According to figures received from Toronto, the number of persons per unit in that city in January this year is only slightly greater than the number in 1940, and undoubtedly is considerably less than the number during the depression. Some people wonder why that is, but the fact is that in Toronto there are many large homes with only a limited number of people living in them.
I never could understand why a fairly well-to-do man with a family of only one or two could occupy a large house and the government neglect or fail to take possession of that house and do something with it, or at least with part of it, in order to provide accommodation. At the same time the government will keep a small home of six rooms away from an owner-generally speaking it is small homes that are involved-when that home is being rented for $20 or $25 a month. The next house is rented for perhaps $35 a month simply because it did not come under the provisions of the ceiling imposed on October 11, 1941.

Emergency Powers
There is something wrong. I know of seven-roomed houses in which one person is living.
I know of some nine-roomed houses with two people living in them. A year or so ago a great furore was raised because a large house in a good part of the city was to be taken over by the city or the government and rerented. That was not done, but the owner of the house thought it was a terrible thing for the government to suggest putting a hand upon his property. The government is constantly putting its hand upon the homes of tire small people, houses with six rooms or less; and people cannot get possession of their own homes.
I should like the hon. gentleman to say what has been done in the city of Toronto in order to ascertain the amount of space available in the larger houses. While I am on my feet, I should like to say something I had not expected an opportunity to say. On the lake front just east of Yonge street there were many large buildings owned by the Royal Canadian Air Force. Some person has said they were not in condition to be used as living quarters, but I am told that was not so, that they had all the necessary plumbing and other fixtures; that they were well heated, and. in fact, provided everything people who were without homes might require. Yet those buildings were torn down and sold about a year ago. Now as I pass on the train I see a large excavation there, as though some commercial or industrial plant is to be erected. I do not see why these buildings could not have been made available to the people of Toronto, and I should like to know what attempt the government has made to ascertain the possibility of obtaining space in some of the larger homes in the city of Toronto.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Casa Loma. -

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I was not speaking of Casa Loma.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Two main points were raised by the hon. member for High Park. In the first place, I understood him to urge that the government should start a policy of compulsorily billeting persons in homes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Oh, no.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
That has not been done so far, and I should! think hon. members on all sides would hesitate before embarking on a policy of that sort. It is drastic treatment to commence at this stage, to begin forcing additional persons into the premises of home owners or home occupiers. I am, quite frankly, a little amazed at this suggestion coming from
a member of a party which seems to favour the removal of controls as rapidly as may reasonably be possible.
The second point raised by the hon. member, as I understand it, has to do with the R.C.A.F. equipment depot in Toronto. That question was explored, and the city health authorities would not permit that property to be used for housing purposes. I understand that it didi not have the proper type of flooring or plumbing accommodation. Therefore it was not suitable, and was dismantled.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: If the hon. member will give me the report from the civic health authorities to that effect I can take up the matter in the proper place. As far as forcing people into private homes is concerned, I do not see much difference between putting people in part of someone else's home, and refusing to let a man get possession of his own home. I do not speak about rehabilitating these houses; I suppose the parliamentary assistant has heard about shared apartments before this.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I have been wondering to what extent the emergency shelter authorities have cooperated with the municipalities and provinces in providing shelter in the sort of buildings about which the hon. member for High Park had been speaking. In the city of North Battleford, Saskatchewan, the provincial government was able to purchase the airport buildings from War Assets Corporation, and they provided some eighty suites, which meant that every veteran in that city was given an opportunity to have a suite of rooms last winter. Perhaps North Battleford is the only city in Canada in that position. I believe a great deal more of that could be done if we had the right kind of cooperation between the housing administration and the provincial and municipal authorities. Those airport buildings were located just a mile outside North Battleford, and they were turned into nice, comfortable suites renting at a reasonable figure. They have provided playgrounds for the children, a recreation hall for the people living there, a store of their own, and all the rest of it; they have a bus line into the city, and they are really enjoying life. It seems to me that more of that sort of thing could be done with some of these airport buildings in other parts of Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
When I was home over the week-end I drove quite a few miles around the city of Toronto taking a look at buildings under construction. I know the appalling housing situation in Toronto, particularly in my own part of the city where so many thou-
Emergency Powers

sands of the working people live. I know how they are crowded, with two or three or four families in a small six-roomed house. I asked myself if the government had a tabulation made of the millions of bricks being used in the construction of theatres, churches and all sorts of other buildings in Toronto. I am not finding any fault with the fact that these other buildings are being constructed, because permits must have been obtained for that construction. But I thought not only of the millions of bricks being used in those buildings but of the thousands of kegs of nails and the millions of feet of lumber; and as I drove around I asked myself which was the most pressing demand on the government: to permit the construction of theatres and churches, which of course are necessary, and many other buildings of that kind which require vast quantities of building materials and the services of many expert bricklayers, carpenters and so forth, or the demand for the construction of houses. I just asked myself whether the government could be conversant with the appalling housing situation in our large cities and, if so, why they permitted these other buildings to be constructed. I am not opposed to their construction, but surely housing comes first in the situation under which the people are struggling to live at the present time.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: To deal, first, with the points raised by the hon. member for North Battleford. some nine different municipalities in Saskatchewan now have emergency shelter units. The number of projects is larger than that, but nine municipalities are involved. The whole programme is worked out in conjunction with the provincial and municipal authorities, and I should be very much surprised if any of those municipalities said they had received any other than excellent cooperation from the emergency shelter authorities. I believe they have.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am willing to give them credit for that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for that. Cooperation is a two-way proposition. It varies with one municipality and another. It is fair to say that, in general, cooperation with municipalities has been very good.
With respect to the points raised by the hon. member for Davenport, it is really a matter of building materials covered under the order in council which is already passed. I would point- out to him that in the production of colourless window glass it would appear that the supply in 1947 will be ade-

quate. I have the figures available with respect to brick but perhaps there is no point in giving them.
To go back to the question which was debated before, namely, construction permit control and the other controls, the matter of construction permits rests with the municipal authorities. I do not know that there is much need to elaborate on that at this time since the order is already passed. If permits were granted for these buildings they were granted by the municipal authorities. I assume the municipal authorities gave the matter complete and proper attention before they granted them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I really cannot understand it, if the municipal authorities, particularly the city of Toronto, are harassed to death for accommodation, and they are. The eviction court in Toronto is a sad place to enter. I go there frequently and listen to the arguments put forward by those who want eviction and those who do not want eviction to take place. It seems to me strange that the municipal authorities would not try first to house their people. To provide homes for the multitudes who are now packed almost like sardines- that is all we can say about it-in unhealthy and dangerous conditions of every description, should be the important thing. I do not want to think the city council and the city authorities in Toronto would give preference to I do not know how many theatres-I passed by a number of them-which have men working on them and piles of lumber and building materials of every description around them. I am not finding fault with their being built, but I am trying to say that housing should have No. 1 priority over everything else to give the people a chance to live under decent conditions.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Before we leave this order in council, there is a question I wish to ask the parliamentary assistant. When the members for Vancouver were in that city during the Easter holidays they met the city council and, among other things, discussed with them the project of buying certain houses in Bremerton in the state of AVashington. Some 1,600 houses were to be floated on barges to Vancouver. Has that deal gone through?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I have some information on that point. There are two or three things about it. First of all, the municipal authorities in the city of Vancouver will not make a contribution to that project. I understand that they are unwilling to do so. They want it done, if it is done, by the dominion government alone. I might add one other

Emergency Powers
thing. There is no evidence whatever that the United States authorities would permit these houses to be taken out of the United States and into Canada. That is another difficulty.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Have inquiries been made about the matter?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: There is one other difficulty. The municipalities will not administer the project. These are the difficulties in the way at the moment. I think I am justified in saying it looks as if they will not be having Bremerton houses.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Surely there must be something wrong here. I had a copy of a letter which was sent by the corporation council of Vancouver to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, I think. From that letter my understanding was that the city was asking for financial assistance from the government. I understand that to>
a certain amount that financial assistance was offered; whether it was sufficient or not I do not know. I am greatly surprised to hear that the city wanted the government to pay all of it. I am almost sure that is not the case.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am sorry I have not the letter and the reply here. The letter was received and replied to in considerable detail by the minister. As I understand it, the city takes the position that it has no authority to expend money on that project. I understand further that the dominion government made the city an offer under which the dominion government would pay $500 per unit of these houses. I am sorry I have not the letter. If I had I would have more detail.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Have inquiries been made of the United States authorities by the Department of Reconstruction and Supply since Easter?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No such inquiries have been made since Easter. The position is that there is no point in making such inquiry until someone assumes the responsibility by bringing these houses in and financing them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The parliamentary assistant said he believed the United States authorities would not release the houses.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No, I did not express it in that way.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: How did the parliamentary assistant express it? What did he mean to convey?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I said there was no evidence that the United States authorities would permit them to be exported, to Canada.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Why does the department not find out whether or not they can be obtained from the United States?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The reason is-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Are the city authorities and members of parliament just wasting their time trying to have this deal put through? The government should at least find out from the United States government whether or not these buildings can be made available.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The United States
government have a prohibition against the export of building material. The reason they .have not been approached since Easter to change that and to make a special exception or do whatever is required under their law to vary it is that no one here is in a position to take the houses. It is still a hypothetical question because no authority here will assume responsibility for taking the houses and putting them in the city of Vancouver and operating them. That question has to be settled first.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Was an approach made to the L'nited States government before Easter? If so, what was the answer given?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Perhaps I can restate it with a little more detail. The'situation at the moment with respect to these Bremerton houses is simply this: the Canadian government or the department is not in a position to make such an approach to the government of another country until it has a bona fide application to import these houses. Such is not yet the case. There is no bona fide application to import these houses.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I suggest that the lead should come from Ottawa. The people on the Pacific coast have found that these houses are available. They have inspected them and are satisfied with them. They cannot go farther until they know whether or not the houses can be obtained. If they cannot be obtained there is no use in wasting more time on the project.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Perhaps I could state it in another way. There is no use in determining a hypothetical question about an import permit from a foreign government until there is some evidence that someone will import houses. So far, in this talk about Bremerton houses, there is no evidence that they are available, and we have been unable to get any real cooperation in the vray of working out an arrangement with the municipal authorities to provide for paying for and operating the houses. That is the situation and the difficulty.
Emergency Powers

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I wish to speak as the member for Vancouver Centre and not as a minister. I happened to go into the matter thoroughly when I was at home during the Easter recess, though unfortunately I was detained from attendance at the meeting at which my hon. friend the member for Vancouver East and others were present, with the city council, to discuss the situation; but the evidence I received was definitely to the effect that the houses were available, provided that the government of Canada gave assurances to the government of the United States that the houses were required and that they would give their blessing to the enterprise., as these houses could be transported to Vancouver, British Columbia. I happen to know Canada fairly well and there is no place in Canada that requires housing to the extent that Vancouver, British Columbia, does. The conditions there are truly and definitely emergent, and I understand that the hon. member for Vancouver East and two of my colleagues, the hon. member for Vancouver North and the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard, were at a conference the other day. My understanding from dispatches which I saw was that one of two officials of the Department of Reconstruction and Supply was to be sent immediately to Vancouver to confer with the Vancouver city council in regard to this condition.
I wish to impress upon the committee the fact that this condition is a truly serious one in Greater Vancouver and that the negotiations, as far as I know, were proceeding most satisfactorily. I am therefore nonplussed, I must say, by the evidence I have heard tonight, because the Vancouver press has continually carried dispatches, and one or other of these two officials is on his way to Vancouver now to discuss these negotiations with the city council of Greater Vancouver in regard to terms for transporting these houses from Bremerton to Vancouver.
As far as I am concerned, I want to have some further explanation, which I shall ask for in the usual constitutional manner, in regard to the lack of progress with reference to these negotiations, which I had hoped would be successful for the sake of people who today need housing, most of them being ex-servicemen, with their dependents, in Greater Vancouver. Our understanding was, after investigation that these houses could be obtained at prices which were from one-third to two-thirds of the prices for which one can build houses today in Canada, including cost of transportation.

I must agree with the hon. member for Vancouver South-I am afraid I am doing it too frequently nowadays-in his representations in regard to this matter, because after all we represent a great city, a great centre, and in this case a great cause, and anything I can do to assist in this way I shall be most happy to do.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not want to pursue this matter further; but, as I have indicated, I am in the same position as the hon. member for Vancouver Centre. My understanding was that these houses were for sale by the government authorities. They are war surplus, I understand, or something of that kind, and no question of the authority for selling them was involved. There are sixteen hundred of them. According to the figures I saw, the price, set down on a serviced lot in Vancouver, was $2,160, which it was said would enable good accommodation to be provided for ten years. I am very much surprised at the information or lack of information which the parliamentary assistant has given us tonight.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Perhaps I should come back to one point in this discussion. First of all, as to the price, I am not in a position to argue that one way or the other. It is wholly unproven figure and is certainly very much below the cost of moving some houses from Dawson Creek to Edmonton. I am not, however, in a position to argue that in detail one way or the other. The whole crux of the matter is very simple. It comes to this, that the municipal authorities in the city of Vancouver took the position that they have no authority to expend municipal funds for the purpose of providing this type of emergency shelter. Whether they have or have not is a question of law, but certainly it is one that they themselves must assume the responsibility for deciding. We here cannot decide it. That is their position. They take the position that the dominion government should pay all the cost. The dominion government has not paid all the cost of these projects with other municipalities, and just what is the position if the dominion government now goes to British Columbia and pays all the cost in Vancouver, after having worked out satisfactory and reasonably workable arrangements with a great number of other municipalities across the dominion where the municipal and dominion authorities cooperated and contributed their portions of the cost and had the buildings made available, and so on?
That is the crux of the whole situation. As for the urgency in Vancouver, no one at all familiar with the situation will fail to agree at once that there is great need for emergency shelter in that city. That is not in issue at all

Emergency Powers
and is not the point. I think the departmental officials are as well aware of that as anyone, and I can do nothing other than wholly agree with the remarks made by hon. members here about the need for shelter in Vancouver. But we must, I think, come to the real difficulty and deal with it. We must face up to it, and it turns simply on the inability to get cooperation from the municipal authorities either to pay for any part of these buildings made available for emergency shelter or to contribute to their cost.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is another case of passing the buck from the government to the municipality. The municipality will pass it back again, and in the meantime the veterans have no place to live in. The parliamentary assistant has said that the city will not underwrite the scheme-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I went farther than "underwrite"; I said, "will not contribute."

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is the department prepared to make an agreement with a private firm or a private individual if they will underwrite the project?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The policy of the emergency shelter authorities has always been to deal with municipal authorities only. When you get to a matter of local administration, and so on, most people will agree that it is absolutely necessary to have the municipal authorities in it. That cooperation has been forthcoming from practically all the municipalities in the country. It has never been the policy to deal with a private individual in making emergency shelter available on the unit basis.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The press report of the interview that was held here with the minister of reconstruction last week by three of the Vancouver members-unfortunately I was unable to return to Ottawa in time for the interview -was as follows, and I am quoting from the Vancouver Province of April 19:
Previously, the Ottawa government had offered to put up $500 per Bremerton house, if Vancouver would underwrite the proposition. Today, Vancouver M.P.'s drew from Mr. Howe the undertaking that the dominion would put up the same amount even if the project were not handled by the city but through a non-profit corporation, with the accent on non-profit.
Is that statement correct, or is it not, because this evening the parliamentary assistant has said that his department will deal only with the municipality?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
All I can say about that is that the policy has been quite clear in the past. There has always been municipal management- of these emergency shelter projects.
This is the first I have ever heard of any suggestion that there would be other than municipal management of the project. That, if it were true, would, of course, involve a complete change of policy and would be something which the minister would have to deal with. I could not authoritatively bind the minister on a matter of policy like that. But [DOT] it certainly is the first suggestion I have ever heard that we have other than municipal administration of this emergency shelter.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The university of British Columbia is administering some emergency shelter.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Yes, that is quite true for special university projects; the provincial university is doing that.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Is not the Canadian Legion doing that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: In Victoria there is a project where the legion takes part in it. They do not administer it themselves. They take part in it with the municipal authorities. There is one other project of a similar nature.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I wish to ask my hon. friend a question. He has made a statement -and no doubt he has made it quite sincerely and honestly-that the municipal authorities of Vancouver rejected this cooperative enterprise. I should like to know how that communication was received and by whom it was signed. Was it signed by the mayor of Vancouver or by any of the civic aldermen of Vancouver? I am entitled to know, I think, as a representative from Vancouver.	.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: And is it since Easter or before?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I can perhaps help to clarify that. I believe there was an amendment proposed to the city charter which was brought up before the Vancouver city council, a suggested amendment that they were to put forward to the provincial authorities giving them the authority to spend money for purposes like this and the city council rejected it.
I think that would be a matter of record in the city council.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: May I ask who that communication came from? Was it the city clerk of Vancouver who made that communication to my hon. friend?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I cannot say who it was that communicated that to the department. I think it will be found that the amendment was beaten by a very close vote of thirteen to twelve, if my memory serves me correctly.
Emergency Powers

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Have you the date?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I am not sure of the date, but I think it was about the middle of April.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
As one of the three members who attended the meetings with the Vancouver city council and with the minister, I must confess that I am a little surprised at hearing the difference in the parliamentary assistant's version of this and what the minister told us. It is apparently in the press, so in speaking I am not breaking any confidence. This Bremerton deal is a most unusual one, because I am quite sure there is no other place on the North American continent where there is a surplus of 40,000 houses, which is the surplus of wartime houses that there is in the state of Washington and Oregon, which were put up for the shipbuilders. They are two and three-bedroom houses. The houses are available at Bremerton in the state of Washington for $400; that is, the house itself, in its present situation, complete with stove, refrigerator and heating equipment. The joker in it is that the houses are not pre-fabs. They cannot be knocked down except for salvage. There is little sale for them because it is not allowed to move such houses along the highways of either the slate of Washington or the state of Oregon. The only way whereby these houses can be moved is by sea on a scow'. Quite a number of United States communities on Puget sound have obtained those houses at $400, floated1 them to their new location, brought them ashore and established them there. Here is the situation in Vancouver. A group of veterans did go down to examine these houses, did get a commitment that 1,600 can be made available if an official approach were made to the United States housing authorities by the proper authorities. None of the prefabricated houses could be bought because obviously the Americans wanted them themselves, but 1,600 of these other houses could be bought for $400 each. The figures quoted by the hon. member for Vancouver East were to the effect that a total of $2,160 would remove these houses from their sites in these wartime industries at Bremerton, float them up the sound to the Fraser river to the city of Vancouver and put them on these lots provided by the city at $100 apiece. Far from these figures not being certified, the city engineer and the city building inspector of Vancouver have checked these figures and agreed that that is a fair estimate. It is all very w'ell to say that the government has not done this in the past. This is certainly an unusual situation, surplus houses available for the one place 
in Canada where the housing situation is more extreme than it is in any other. We met the Vancouver housing association, that excellent group of citizens who have so well managed the hotel Vancouver where 1,227 veterans' families are now finding shelter.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is the citizens' rehabilitation council.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Yes,
which has done such fine work. It is quite true, that unlike Wartime Housing, these Bremerton houses when set up will not be the type of housing that could be sold to the tenants as can Wartime Housing. I have gone over these matters carefully with the alderman who is most concerned, Aider-man Cornett, and these young veterans, and I think this project should be publicly underwritten. If the city cannot do it, then it should be done by the federal government.
As far as the statement made by the parliamentary assistant is concerned, that the Vancouver city council rejected the scheme, that is not quite true. Six out of eight councillors were extremely anxious that the city should take advantage of this unusual offer. Two of the councillors, however, when this matter was brought up before the council, insisted on the regular two-weeks' notice before a charter amendment could be proposed. By that time the provincial legislature had prorogued, so that there was no opportunity. It is interesting to note that the mayor of Vancouver who is such an authority on spending other people's money did not raise bis voice to try to help the six aldermen get this housing authority through. In fairness to the Vancouver aider-men, six of these aldermen did try very hard to get the city to purchase these houses. I suggest, like the other Vancouver members, that this is a most unusual situation where these good houses are available at such a low price, and that certainly no buck-passing between the federal government and the city council or any other group should be allowed to stand in the way.
As far as the statement of the parliamentary assistant is concerned, I was present at the meeting when the minister of reconstruction did say that he had made an offer of a grant of $500 per unit if these Bremerton houses were brought in by the city so that there must have been some pretty definite plan submitted to him before he would make such an offer. On the question raised by my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver East, the hon. member for Vancouver-Bur-rard and myself, as to whether that offer would be extended to a non-profit group, he

Emergency Powers
did not quite commit himself. He said he was inclined to recommend it if it were a responsible non-profit organization, but that he would have to consult his colleagues before committing the government. I think at that time he suggested the Vancouver housing association or the rehabilitation league, who have done such excellent work. Far from saying no, I think it is a fair statement to say that he was inclined to approve if some responsible group would take over the importation of these houses.
This does not immediately concern me, because I am not a Vancouver member, although my constituency is called Vancouver North. It does, however, concern every member from British Columbia to see an offer like this of 1,600 houses, with stove, heater and refrigerator, available at $400, with an estimate of a total cost of importation and erection of between $2,000 and $2,500, slide by, because of some jurisdictional quarrel over who should pay for emergency shelter.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I have listened to this discussion in silence, but with a great deal of interest. Here we have a case where, as I understand it, the city council is afraid of getting into subsidized low-rental housing all alone, without any help from the province or the dominion. We have heard from the parliamentary assistant and from the other hon. members for about half an hour, that the dominion and the city council cannot find a basis for agreement. I believe that is what worries private members from Vancouver- the fact that agreement cannot be reached.
There is no question in the world that we must have a large number of houses built this year in Vancouver by Wartime Housing, and probably we should have the Bremerton houses, too. I do not care what agreement is come to, but I wish to say to the parliamentary assistant that very soon now these houses must be made available. This very same dispute between the dominion and the city had held up the opening of the old Vancouver hotel as a veterans hostel for some six months. The need was most acute. Many hon. members'-and I was one of them-were active in trying to get it open. Late in January it was opened, but because certain veterans took forcible possession of the hotel. When that was done all the difficulties were resolved, satisfactory arrangements were made and the hotel was opened. While I am not sure of my dates, I believe it was six or eight months later the Little Mountain camp was declared surplus and evacuated. It, like the old hotel Vancouver, remained vacant for a considerable
period of time, while this same dispute was going on. The inevitable happened there, too.
I could liken the inevitable to air rushing into a vacuum. There were empty houses on the one hand, and veterans' families in sore need on the other. The veterans simply moved in to Little Mountain. Had it not been for the university authorities, and had not the university branch of the legion come to the rescue very smartly and taken over that project on a management basis, at the same time straightening out the difficulties caused by the "squatting", if I may use a term which has been widely used, there would have been trouble at that point. The people of Vancouver have not liked the experience in these two instances.
I have risen at this time, at the end of this long and indeterminate discussion, to express my view that the government cannot let that happen again. I do not care what the arrangement is. I do not care even if the management is provided, without a detailed agreement with the city having been reached, such agreement being left to be decided after.
I should like to impress upon the government that this contract for the old hotel comes to an end early in 1948. There are at least 2,500 veterans' families urgently requiring housing at once. We cannot let any more emergency shelter become vacant without having management ready to take it over on the very day it becomes vacant. And we cannot let these 1,600 Bremerton houses go by, unless we are prepared next April to have a sufficient number of houses on the ground so that no one will miss the 1,600 we might have got from Bremerton.
I know Wartime Housing is working much faster now, as it acquires what is called the know-how of building. I am much concerned about the 2,000 houses mentioned in the newspaper report. The first contract was for 1,200 houses, and that was signed in the summer of 1945. I believe the last few houses are either just now coming into occupation, or have just come into occupation since the beginning of the year. I do not believe we have a period of even one or two months to play with before some actual work must be done to get wartime housing or Bremerton houses into Vancouver.
My suggestion to the parliamentary assistant is this: You have reached an impasse with the city council. They are on ground on which they consider they are entitled to stand. You are on ground on which you consider you are entitled to stand. We shall never get anywhere that way. You will both have to give way to some extent, in the interests of
Emergency Powers

the people who need those houses^ no matter what it may do to your other arrangements, and no matter what it may do to the city's responsibility for housing in the future. Both sides will have to come together, prepared to give way, so as to get those houses started.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
One or two things I think should be said about this point, although some of it may be repetitious. First of all, I think I made it clear in answer to the Minister of Veterans Affairs that there is no doubt at all about the need for emergency shelter in Vancouver. It was said tonight that the need in that city was the most extreme in Canada. That is not quite accurate. In any event it is extreme, and there is no doubt about the urgency.
The term buck-passing was used in reference to the negotiations in an effort to get emergency shelter in there. I think the kindest remark I can make about that term is that it is most unhelpful.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It is most true, too.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
It is most untrue, as well as being unhelpful, notwithstanding the hon. member for Vancouver South. When a dominion authority, which has a responsibility to all the people of Canada in all the municipalities, finds an arrangement that is satisfactory to all the municipalities in Canada, with possibly one exception in addition to Vancouver, an arrangement into which almost all municipalities have seen fit to enter, and about which they have been satisfied-and have so expressed themselves in many instances-surely it is not buck-passing to ask the municipality of Vancouver to enter into a similar type of arrangement, and to start off the suggestion by offering them a cash contribution, right off, in the first letter, for each housing unit. Surely it is not buckpassing to suggest that the municipality look after the local administration of an emergency housing project? If all other municipalities have seen fit to enter into this arrangement, how can we now be accused of non-cooperation when we are asking the city to enter into the same type of arrangement. It just is not logical or reasonable.
Something was said about the private feelings of the city councillors. I am sorry, but I am not in position to tell hon. members what are the feelings of the city councillors because I do not know their private feelings. I merely know the position they have taken publicly in the course of their duties; I merely know the position they have seen fit to maintain, rightly or wrongly, as city councillors. I have not even suggested that they were wrong; I have merely stated the position they
[Mr. Merritt. 1
took, and that is their affair. They have their responsibilities; they have their own jurisdiction, and I have not been critical of it at all. I have merely pointed out what it was.
It will be seen from the discussion tonight that, notwithstanding the speeches of hon. members, notwithstanding their intense interest in having emergency shelter provided for needy cases, we come back to the same point, that not one of them has dealt with the key problem, whether or not it is possible to do anything without the cooperation of the municipal authorities.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I most certainly have done so.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I do not want to enter into a detailed discussion. I should like to ask hon. members who controls such things as water connections, the distribution of water and the disposal of sewage in the corporation limits?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The city is not raising any trouble about servicing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: They will not give the services that all other municipalities give in connection with wartime housing. By the way, there are a great many of these units going into Vancouver. Their proposition at the moment is that the city be paid $400 for each lot upon which wartime houses have been built.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is w'hat Wartime Housing promised to do and now you are reneging on it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No, I am not reneging on anything; I am merely stating the fact. That was in addition to requesting that full taxes be paid on all these lots.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Why not?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is the difficulty there. The emergency shelter authorities are fully aware of the difficulty in Vancouver and are most anxious and willing to cooperate. However the government has a duty to other persons residing outside the city of Vancouver, and it has to defend what it does in one municipality when it is different from what is done in other municipalities.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
As a member on this side of the house and also as a member who is not representing a Vancouver seat, perhaps I can be expected to make a little more impartial reply. One of the points raised by the parliamentary assistant explains

Emergency Powers
why the Vancouver city council feels so dubious about going on. Wartime Housing made an agreement with Vancouver by which they got these lots very cheaply and for low taxes. The signed agreement was that if any house was sold to tenants within five years the city would get $400 as tax sale price of the lot. Now when the houses are beginning to be sold Wartime Housing is attempting to renegotiate the contract, which the city accepted in good faith, to give only $100.
When three of the Vancouver members met the minister we said that one [DOT] of the first things that should be done to establish the right atmosphere for negotiation between council and government was for Wartime Housing to live up to their present agreement and pay the S400 they had agreed to pay.
The second point in connection with these negotiations came out in the words of the parliamentary assistant when he said that there were a very great number of wartime houses in Vancouver. That is quite true. In my own riding of Vancouver North we have a. great number of them which were built on lots that were obtained for $1 a lot. Twenty-five dollars was paid in lieu of taxes, which means that the citizens of Vancouver North, who were paying $75 or $80 more taxes on a similar type of house on lots in the immediate vicinity, were making up the difference.
The three Vancouver members made it quite clear to the minister that they did not believe in going on giving special subsidies to veterans in wartime houses by continuing to pay $25 in lieu of taxes. We felt that the veteran who bought a house privately should receive some protection. Why should he pay full taxes on his house and then share the cost of the reduction in taxes to veterans in wartime houses? The three of us, despite our different political outlooks, agreed that the Vancouver city council was right. I would suggest to the parliamentary assistant, as we suggested, to the minister of reconstruction, that one of the first things Wartime Housing bad better do in Vancouver is to live up to the deal that they have made.
Mr. MelLRAITH: As far as the contract between Wartime Housing and Vancouver is concerned, Wartime Housing is perfectly willing and ready and anxious to live up to its contract in detail. If the hon member want to pursue the point any farther he will find that there has never been the slightest suggestion that they do other than live up to the contract.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Apparently the parliamentary assistant is right and
the mayor and the council are wrong, or Wartime Housing is doing something of which the parliamentary assistant has no knowledge. The first point brought up by the Vancouver members-there were four of us at that meeting-was the fact that Wartime Housing were trying to renegotiate that stipulation, and I ask my colleagues to substantiate that statement.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
That is true.
Mr. MelLRAITH: I think I can clear that up very quickly. If the city wants full taxes on these houses it must renegotiate the contract with Wartime Housing, because the contract provides, among other things, for a much smaller fixed payment in lieu of taxes. If the city wants its full taxes it must, of course, renegotiate the agreement. It cannot have both sides of the same coin face uppermost at the same time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: All this discussion just goes to show that there is need for people to reach an understanding. I must say that I would rather not thresh over this old straw: I would much rather hear from the parliamentary assistant that he realizes that these houses must go into Vancouver this year and that he is prepared, through Wartime Housing, to see that they do go there and that an agreement is reached by such negotiation as is necessary. If the city proves intractable, as the parliamentary assistant seems to suggest, then the suggestion the Vancouver members have already made should be adopted, that is, that the rents be set slightly higher to take the difference into consideration. There is no good in trying to allot the blame, and it would not be necessary if we could be satisfied that the government was intent on getting these houses started. If that were the case we would not have to discuss this matter at all.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Two subjects have become mixed up in the discussion. One is the ordinary wartime houses and the other is this Bremerton project. I have my notes covering Wartime Housing which I took at the meeting with the city council, and we were certainly told by the city council that the original arrangement was that if the houses were sold within five years the city would get $400 a house.
Mr. MelLRAITH: That is correct.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
We saw them during the Easter recess and they told us that the government was then taking the stand that, instead of paying $400, only $100 would be paid.
I also took some notes with regard to the Bremerton project. The parliamentary assist-
Emergency Powers

ant has said1 the city would not give any help at all. The councillors toldi us the city would open up the district in which the Bremerton houses would be placed, at the expense of the city, which I presume meant roads and water, at least; and they also said they would either give or renit the lots to the Central Mortgage Corporation, whichever the corporation wished. So that there is no question about the council being willing to cooperate. It is just a matter of the two authorities getting together.
I would ask the parliamentary assistant whether his department will now find) out from the United States government whether these houses are available for sale to Canada. That has not been done as yet, and I suggest that it should be done just as quickly as possible. Perhaps it will have to be done through the Department of External Affairs. The minister of that department is here this evening, and he can tell us whether that step will be necessary. Is the government willing to find out at once whether or not these houses are available? And is the Department of Reconstruction willing to have the houses, when they are brought in, operated by an organization such as the citizens' rehabilitation council or some other non-profit organization? If those two points were cleared up, first, whether or not the houses can be obtained at all from the United States, and whether, if they are brought in, they could be operated by a body such as the rehabilitation council, we would be getting somewhere.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard raised some questions about the speed with which these problems are handled. I believe the emergency shelter authorities and the department are fully equipped to deal very quickly with these matters; the difficulty does not lie in that direction at all.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: May I ask the parliamentary assistant when you would have to commence in order to have 2,000 wartime houses completed by next April?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I cannot answer that question accurately; too many factors are involved, so that any answer I might give would not be worked out carefully enough.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That rather destroys the value of what the parliamentary assistant just said.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
No, it does not destroy it at all; it just shows the need of cooperation on the part of all parties concerned. The

situation is still the same on this point as I previously stated it to be. The question has been raised of the application to the United States authorities. I will bring the matter before the minister, but for myself, with what little influence I have, I certainly would not suggest that an application be made to a foreign government to import houses on a hypothetical question like this, when no one is ready to import them and the authority is not clarified.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: You would not even ask whether the United States would consent?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Surely we must have some evidence of a bona fide application to import before a foreign government can be approached on a matter like this. However, as I said, I will bring forward the point in any event. The question was narrowed down by the hon. member for Vancouver South in his concluding remarks in regard to the management of these houses, assuming the other difficulties were worked out in conjunction with the city. He asked whether the citizens' rehabilitation council could administer them, or whether that might be done by some other authority. In the first place, "some other authority" is perhaps pretty vague, and I think we can just leave that aside for the moment. As far as the citizens' rehabilitation council is concerned, I should think possibly some satisfactory arrangement could be worked out for the management of this project by them, if all the other difficulties could be satisfactorily solved in cooperation with the city. I do not think there is any use in beating over the other point of where the city councillors stand or do not stand. The fact remains that they claim they have no authority to spend any money on getting these houses in, and the further fact remains that they have declined to apply for that authority. As I said1 before, I have been careful not to state whether they are right or wrong in that; I merely give it as the fact.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The members from the Vancouver area have I think, done a very good job. I was in Vancouver at the time the discussions took place between the Vancouver members and the city council, and the statement by the parliamentary assistant tonight comes as quite a surprise to me. In reading the Vancouver newspapers, one got the impression that the city fathers were prepared to cooperate fully in carrying out a project of this kind. I believe Vancouver deserves special consideration. My information is that a larger percentage of ex-service personnel have settled in Vancouver than in any other

Emergency Powers
city in the country. I think it is well established that building materials are going to be very short for the next couple of years, and with the situation described' by the hon. member for Vancouver North, where 1,600 houses can be placed on lots in Vancouver with very little trouble, I believe, while this government has this emergency power, it should go out of its way to see that something is done. I believe the hon. member for Vancouver South made a reasonable request when he suggested that the minister of reconstruction should1 consult with the United States authorities to find out whether or not these houses can be made available. If the Vancouver newspapers were reporting the conferences at all accurately I am sure public opinion in Vancouver will force the city fathers to go along with the federal authorities in reaching some agreement. The whole discussion thus far this evening emphasizes the point I made on Friday, that we do need to have consultation at all levels of government; and I think the parliamentary assistant should give some assurance that machinery will be set up to enable us to deal with this sort of problem.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I was in Quebec last September making a survey in regard to the question of a free port, and on the docks there I saw a number of prefabricated houses. On inquiry I was advised that they were being shipped to France, and I was very glad to learn that France was getting some assistance from us. I understood that we were sending a thousand or more prefabricated houses, each having about four rooms. They were neat little houses; as a Canadian I was very proud of them and was glad to think our allies were getting some assistance. At the same time I wondered if we had so many houses in Canada that we could afford to ship a thousand or so abroad in that way.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The hon. member for Mackenzie raised a point as to cooperation. Perhaps the best answer to that is that we have approximately 120 of these emergency shelter projects, and we get very good cooperation in connection with at least 117 of them. I think that emphasizes the degree of cooperation the authorities are prepared to give in this matter. There is no doubt at all that the utmost cooperation is required on the part of all the authorities, whether dominion or municipal.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Can the parliamentary assistant say anything about prefabricated houses being shipped from Vancouver to England?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: To deal with the second point raised by the hon. member for Davenport about prefabricated houses, it is quite true that prefabricated houses were being exported, but they were only shells with the lumber in them. They had none of the finishing materials in them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No stoves; no plumbing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: No, nothing of that kind at all; no wiring or anything of that sort; just the lumber shells, and the lumber in them is actually taken out of the lumber export quota. It is part of the export quota of lumber.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Something has been said about the question of houses in the city of Toronto. So far as emergency shelter and shared accommodation are concerned, many people in Toronto would be glad to take people in.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: They generally do.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I know, but you are easy to take in. People in Toronto are willing to take persons in and give them shelter. A great deal of that is being done at the present time, especially in connection with university students. But you have to be careful who they are. They have to be compatible. That is to say, they have to be people who can get on together. There are two reasons why the people would like to do it. We realize the appalling situation we have in Toronto. If hon. members were there they would realize it too. It is easy enough to get these people into your houses. They will come; there is no doubt about that. All you have to do is to ask them to come and the}" will come in; but they will stay there, and it is quite a problem to get them out, particularly when you think of the regulations in connection with evictions and all the long processes which have to be gone through. The average person who has a house is going to be just a little bit careful before he takes anybody in. My suggestion is, make some change in the law in connection with eviction. Make it easier for a person to get rid of these people if they are not liked. Change it so that they can be evicted for cause. At the present time it is difficult to get rid of them for cause. I know of home owners who have been trying to get rid of these people for cause and they have not been able to get them out.
I suggest that if we have some sort of written agreement between a person who owns a house and the person who wishes to come in, which would be binding and which could not be overriden by the present order in council with regard to agreements, it will be
Emergency Powers

found that a great many people in Toronto will be glad to give accommodation to those who need emergency shelter. That is an important factor. People will not take persons into their homes and give them shelter today because it is so difficult to get them out. Unless they are almost crooks you can hardly get them out of your house. That is the suggestion I have to make. I do not like the idea of blaming Toronto for lack of shelter or the citizens for not giving shelter to these people because it is not the fault of the citizens. It is the fault of the regulations governing evictions.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It is the fault of the government.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It is the fault of the government, yes. The hon. member did not think I was speaking on behalf of the government. Perhaps I have not expressed myself clearly but I think I have made my point. My suggestion to the parliamentary assistant is to do something about these regulations and he will find that a great many homes will be opened up.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
In games it is often wise to get an out-of-town referee who is unprejudiced toward these aristocrats from British Columbia. They assume that position with the rest of Canada all the time. In the private quarrel which has been going on between them and the parliamentary assistant to the minister I am trying to analyse the facts. I accept it on all sides that in Bremerton, which is not far away, there are 1,600 houses available, which could be brought to Vancouver and set up-they contain a refrigerator and a stove-for approximately $2,000. That seems to be the basic fact. If that can be done it is the cheapest housing in the world for Canada, infinitely less than we are paying under any other government scheme. What is the reason for this debate and what is the position of the parliamentary assistant? Merely one of frustration, saying we cannot do it because of some people-I was going to use the word "stupid"-perhaps stubborn people on the Vancouver city council. Here we sit in this House of Commons which is assumed to be a responsible and deliberative body. That last word is certainly true. Here we sit w'ith a thing at our doorstep which should be done, and we find the parliamentary assistant-all the committee wants it done- saying we cannot do it because of a technical -and it is a technical-difficulty with the Vancouver city council. That being so, it is not good enough for the parliamentary assistant to tell us that our hands are tied for that

reason, without giving us some constructive suggestion as to how this difficulty can be solved.
Then I turn to the second question which was asked by all the Vancouver members as to the present status of these houses. By "status" I mean whether or not these houses can still be purchased. The parliamentary assistant takes the position-where he gets the authority or the precedent for it I do not know-that he will not ask the government of the United States-I assume from that remark that the houses are governmental owmed-whether they are available until he has bad the detail of purchase and movement worked out. If business were conducted in that way we would never get anywhere. Surely there is no object in fiddling with the city council of Vancouver. There is no object in blaming them for being stubborn if these houses are not available. All we have to do is ask a very simple question. I understand from the hon. member from Vancouver North that the only reason we can get them is that you have to float them. They are not prefabricated, and Vancouver is one of the places to which they can be floated. . With the greatest respect to the parliamentary assistant, his every answer, his whole speech tonight, was simply that of frustration, saying, "blame it on the other fellow," without a single constructive suggestion as to how we can get the 1.600 houses which are so badly needed by men returned from this war. In other words, the answer is not good enough.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Most of the debate this evening has centred around houses to be built in the cities. I have on previous occasions pointed out the desirability of erecting houses where there is work for men to do- in the country. As far as British Columbia is concerned, we need to erect houses near the logging camps and sawmills. I understood last year that the regulations were made more elastic, so that logging, mining and fishing companies might be able to get assistance in the construction of houses in those areas away from the city. I was concerned with the remarks made by the parliamentary assistant this evening, as far as I could hear him, and his voice at that time did not carry very well to these back benches here. Did he say that only the municipalities could administer houses built under these schemes?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Under the emergency shelter.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I was under the impression that, according to the regulations amended last year, logging, lumbering, fishing and min-

Emergency Powers
ing companies would be able to erect and administer houses, assisted in the financing by this federal government.
Mr. McliLRAITH: I was speaking about emergency shelter.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I should, like to ask the parliamentary assistant how many such projects have been started since these regulations were passed last session.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The hon. member for Nanaimo has been, I am afraid, inadvertently confusing what is before the committee at the moment. We are now dealing with the emergency shelter regulations and my remarks were confined to them. The point he now raises has to do with the National Housing Act and administration of Wartime Housing Limited. There is on the order paper a resolution concerning the National Housing Act and I hope we shall reach it soon, when the information he asks for can be given to him. The question he asks does not pertain to the emergency shelter regulations.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Will the two orders in council referring to emergency shelter carry?
P.C. 9439 and P.C. 7502 agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: With regard to order in council No. 3, an amendment has been offered but not accepted. There have however been amendments offered and accepted to No. 245 and No. 1997. Will these two orders in council as amended carry?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
This afternoon the parliamentary assistant was kind enough to promise me that he would make inquiries into a situation which has already considerably vexed the house and, I understand, the minister, and that is the matter of nails. Since the matter was last discussed in the house, I have had telegrams from farmers and ranchers in my own constituency saying that they require to do their spring work on their flumes for irrigation purposes. Unless they get nails to repair these flumes the water will not reach the land, and in that dry country it is essential that irrigation be started now. It is absolutely impossible to obtain nails. There is, we are advised, no priority for such purposes as repairing flumes; the only priority that exists is with respect to the building of houses, but I am told that, even after this priority is satisfied, there are nails left over. Although we are advised of all these factors, I had a second telegram today informing me that no nails are available except on the black market, and on calling this matter to the attention of the department I am given to understand that there exists an unexplainable .situation in British Columbia with regard to 83166-160
the disappearance of nails from legitimate markets. Has the parliamentary assistant had those inquiries made which he promised, and is he in a position to tell me how I can assist these farmers in getting nails which they require for the repair of their flumes?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
