speechtext: The hon. member for Kamloops didi speak to me about this matter this afternoon. I gave what information I had and I was to speak to him further before six o'clock. I told him I would see him this evening but I have not had an opportunity of doing so, as hon. members will appreciate.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I appreciate that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: The situation is this. The priorities given for nails are limited to the low-cost houses under the Veterans' Land Act, Wartime Housing, integrated housing, and veterans housing of that sort, and it leaves between eighty and eighty-five per cent of the gross nail production in the country available for distribution through the normal channels of trade. Apparently there has been a severe difficulty in some parts of British Columbia in getting nails through the local hardware stores. I dto not think there is any doubt about that difficulty and the acuteness of it. There is no control of the distribution down through the retail outlets. There is simply control over all production and the nails required for priority projects. The steel controller is at present in western Canada. Perhaps all I can usefully say on the point is that the difficulty spoken of by the hon. member for Kamloops will be looked into.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I appreciate the position the department is in and also the spirit of the remarks made by the parliamentary assistant, but I think he on his part will appreciate my difficulty. These people want twenty-five kegs of nails in Ashcroft. They need them urgently for this work, because if they do not get the water in that country in the spring, and get it on the land, they will not have any crops at all. All the flumes are knocked to pieces every winter by the snow and ice; they are only wooden structures which have to be made watertight every year. The people on whose behalf I am speaking want twenty-five kegs of nails, and the sympathetic and courteous remarks of the parliamentary assistant, while I sincerely appreciate them, will not help me to tell them how to get nails. Surely the department can bring some pressure to bear upon those who are in charge of the wholesale distribution of nails in that province. I am not one to do any capitalist-baiting or business-baiting, because business as a whole is, I believe, respectable, and has been pushed

Emergency Powers

around too much; but there are two firms-* McLennan, McFeely and Prior and Marshall-Wells-who largely control or influence the wholesale distribution of hardware in that province, and I am quite sure they would be anxious to adjust the situation which is portrayed by the parliamentary assistant, who says that only fifteen per cent of the nails are allocated on a priority basis, which means that eighty-five per cent are available for normal trade. If these firms had it brought home to them that nails are going astray I am sure they would make twenty-five kegs available to those in Ashcroft who need them. As a matter of fact, I have no doubt that if it were brought to their attention that people all through the interior of the province, the retail hardware stores, cannot get nails except on the black market, these: responsible firms would look into the matter and make sure that hardware stores in the interior of the province get their fair share of nails direct from their warehouse. Will the parliamentary assistant say whether the department can use their influence-I hate asking them to use it, but the nails are needed-and send a telegram to Marshall-Wells and McLennan, McFeely and Prior, asking them to make twenty-five kegs of nails of the specified size available to the Ashcroft Ranchers' Association?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I intended to do something more than express myself sympathetically to the hon. member for Kamloops. I do not feel myself in a position to send a telegram to the wholesaler. I did indicate that the steel controller, who is also the priorities officer, is in the west now, and we also have a regional officer in Vancouver. I meant to imply that we would certainly look further into the difficulty raised by my hon. friend. I refrained from saying that any priority order will be issued, because it will not be issued. What we can do is to make an inquiry to see where we are likely to get the nails, to find out where they have been trying to get the nails and get all the other relevant information. We simply have not all that available here at the moment. The best I can do for the hon. member is simply to indicate that the matter will be looked into further by the appropriate officer, with a view to helping him and indicating where the nails should be available.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Can the action be initiated by telegraph now, so that the investigation will start first thing tomorrow morning?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I may be overcautious, Mr. Chairman, but I do not care to tie myself down as to the method or the time. I do not know whether certain officials in the depart-

ment will be talking by telephone with the steel controller tomorrow or not, or how it will be done.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Have his secretary dictate a telegram.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I suggest to the hon. member that lie leave the matter just with the statement I made, that we would have it looked into. That means precisely what it said. If he would just leave it that way, perhaps he would get done by me what he is hoping to get done. I can only say that I can direct the inquiry to the proper officials who can get the facte, find out what the situation is and try to be as helpful as they can.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this atmosphere of frustration is spreading.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I suggest to the parliamentary assistant that he go a little farther because, when I was back home at Easter time, it was drawn to my attention that farmers who were living close to the boundary and who were unable to get nails, were able to buy across the line all the Canadian nails they required at more than double the price. This is an aspect which has never before been brought to the attention of the committee, and I am doing it now. These farmers living within about ten or twelve miles from the border, who were unable to find nails in Canada, went across the border in their cars and, lo and behold, in the hardware stores in the cities and towns close to the border there were kegs of Canadian nails. It is well known that the United States authorities have withdrawn about thirty-four customs officers. I know the department cannot stop the taking of nails across the line, but this is what is worrying us: [DOT] How did these bootleggers get the nails in the first instance? How were they able to get kegs of nails which are now in the United States and being sold at two and a half times the price?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Are they Canadian nails?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Canadian nails. They went across the border under cover, but how were they obtained? What wholesaler supplied these black market men with Canadian nails so that they were able to do this nefarious business? It is galling now for Canadians, when they cannot get nails in their own country, to go across to the United States and find Canadian-made nails right in the shops in the United States.
I had another case of a young veteran who could not get nails, where a contractor said to him, "I can get you some;" and the

Emergency Powers
contractor sent to the province of Saskatchewan and got him two kegs of nails. How have they a surplus in Saskatchewan? He told me that on good authority. He said, "It is true that I paid double the price for them, but I wanted those nails and I got them." When the parliamentary assistant is having the matter looked into I suggest that he find out, or have instructions given to find out, first, how these nails are slipping across the line and, second, who is responsible for handing out nails to these men who are carrying on this nefarious business.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Were the Saskatchewan
nails black market nails?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
No. So far as I know, the
Saskatchewan nails were not; but the Canadian nails across the line were black market nails.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I have heard some hon. members say that they realize the government's difficulty. I can say that I understand the government's muffing. We hear about nails for veterans' homes, but we hear nothing very much about the shortage of steel for ships, of which this country is badly in need. When we cannot build ships we have unemployment, particularly in Collingwood, Kingston or any other city in Canada where ships are being constructed. This entire situation has been laid at the feet of the government and blamed on them. Possibly we should extend the numbers who are granted O.B.E.'s and a few other honours, to make this government wake up and do the job which they did during the war when shortages occurred. There seems to be a lack of incentive to get down to earth and get busy.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: More controls.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
We do not need controls. I 'have had hundreds of men working for me, and I always found that if you talked to them as mem, on a commonsense basis, they would increase their working hours and produce the goods; and1 it was not C.C.F. controls that did that. There must be a solution. I have found this to be true of union officials, union men, labouring men and women all over this country: if appealed to properly and if the shortage was actually demonstrated to them conclusively, they would get down to work and produce the goods. I believe that is applicable to any. plant in Canada producing any commodity.
We continually harp from day to day on the shortage of nails-bootleg nails made in Canada, bought in the United States and used in Canada. You skip over the shortage of 83166-1601
steel for all purposes, and that is due to the government's negligence prior to the cessation of hostilities. Eighteen months before this war was over, when the Germans were retreating in France, the minister of reconstruction knew that the war would be over very shortly; and if he can point his finger to any preparation that he, his department or this government made to meet the exigencies which exist today in any commodities, I should like him to do so. The people of Canada are being hoodwinked about the shortage of nails. But in every single commodity there has been no preparation made to alleviate these shortages. We are spending days here trying to extend the powers, for what? Powers to procrastinate. That is what we are doing. Let us get down to earth. We have spent an hour tonight listening to members from Vancouver who could not get a concrete statement out of the parliamentary assistant about what he was actually going to do or what this government was going to do, so that there could be a concrete and definite comeback from the officials of Vancouver city. Talk about buckpassing! It is all buck-passing. Possibly we should offer more O.B.E.'s, and then we might get somewhere with the production of all the shortages which exist today.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I should like to say a very few words about the position of Nova Scotia in respect of timber control. That will get us off steel for a few minutes.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Let the parliamentary
assistant go out and send my telegram first.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: On a point of order, may I ask what we are discussing.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I called the orders in council with regard to both the steel and timber regulations, because the amendment with respect to both regulations had been approved. However, if the committee would prefer to dispose of the steel regulation first, we can do so.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: You have not yet disposed of order in council P.C. 3.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That order in council stands until we dispose of 245 and 1997, because amendments in respect of those two orders in council have been passed. I thought the committee should come back to pass the amendment to P.C. 3.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: It was my understanding that we would pass these one after another, and P.C. 3 would follow the emergency shelter orders in council.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
It is immaterial, so far as the chair is concerned. I shall read the
Emergency Powers

amendment. It is moved by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction :
That the following be inserted in the schedule to the act in the column entitled "Amendments" so as to pertain to order in council P.C. 3 of 4th January, 1944, as amended:
"Section 12(2) is deleted and the following substituted therefor:
12(2) Where a controller believes that any person has failed to 'produce books, records or documents, or to give full and complete information as required by such controller under tjie authority of any regulation, he may, with the approval of a judge-of the Exchequer Court of Canada or of a superior or a county court, which approval such judge is hereby empowered to give upon the ex parte application of the controller, authorize in writing under his hand a police officer, police constable or other person employed for the preservation and maintenance of the public peace, together with any other person named therein, to enter and search, if necessary by force, any building, receptacle or place, for books, records or documents which may contain information required by such controller, and to seize the same and carry them before such controller or such other person as such controller may direct, to be held at the discretion of such controller for such uses as he is authorized by any regulation to make."
Amendment agreed to.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Shall P.C. 3 as amended carry?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I asked the Minister of Justice if he would accept an amendment to section 15 (6) of P.C. 3. The minister pointed out at that time that there were certain objections to the amendment, one being that the same provision occurred in an earlier order in council, and that the amendment had been omitted when that order was discussed.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Would the hon. member for Kamloops let us have the section of P.C. 3 to which he is referring?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
It is 15 (6). The amendment which I should like to move is as follows:
That the schedule to the bill be amended by inserting in the column headed "Amendments" the following:
"Order in council P.C. 3 dated January 4, 1944, as amended, is further amended by deleting from section 15 (6 the words "or is found or apprehended or in custody" where they occur in the last line thereof."
The purpose, as I said the other night, was to provide that a person must be sued or proceeded against in the place where he carries on business or where he resides. That ensures that there will be no abuse of the power of prosecution in taking action which might result, as the section is at present worded, in a man's being apprehended in one part of the country, although he carries on
[The Chairman.]
business in another part, and being held and proceeded against at some point thousands of miles away from his place of business without his books and records available.
The Minister of Justice pointed out that a similar provision existed in the Foreign Exchange Control Board Act which passed the house last year. He said we had not taken specific objection to that section, and upon investigation I find that is true. However I do not think the fact it is in that act makes it necessarily good. The Secretary of State for External Affairs pointed out that it does not make it necessarily bad, but I think he will agree it does not make it necessarily good. It also exists in the Customs Act. But there it is clearly confined to cases where the penalty will not exceed S200. The penalty here may be as high as $5,000.
The government says it is making an effort to do away with controls as rapidly as possible. In many instances it has consented to restrictions on wide and possibly excessive powers within the framework of the main control measures. It is on this ground I would ask that the amendment be accepted.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I am afraid I am in
a position of not being able to accept the amendment offered by the hon. member for Kamloops. These words have been contained in the section for some years. We are now dealing with an extension for a limited period of time. So far there has been no complaint about this section. If the words are taken out we are faced with the possible administrative difficulty of having to go to the expense of transporting an accused person back to the place where the offence was committed, or where he carries on business, even though the accused might be prepared to plead guilty.
Mr. ST. LAURENT:	The same provision
is in the order which was passed with regard to the wartime prices and trade board. If the hon. member will look at page 26 of the office consolidation and refer particularly to section 11(2) of that order, which was passed by the committee the other day, he will find exactly the same language.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I admit that, but I pointed out that it was an oversight. Had we noticed it, we would have moved a similar amendment when that order in council was before the house. As to the matter of expense, if an accused is prepared to plead guilty, surely it would not cost any more to commence the action in the court where the accused resides or carries on business. If he is going to plead guilty, presumably he would not

Emergency Powers
object to that being done. It would not cost any more, or present any administrative difficulty.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Earlier this evening
hon. members raised questions about breaches of these orders. By deleting these words the hon. member is making it more difficult administratively to determine where offences take place, and permitting the raising of jurisdictional defences to prosecutions in what is already a difficult administrative position. I can only reiterate that this is an inopportune time to make that administrative change.
We have precedents of this sort in the permanent legislation, and I do not see why we should be expected to make the exception in this temporary short-term order in council, when we have it in permanent legislation. There has never been any suggestion that it has been in any way abused, in the number of years when there were a great many control orders outstanding.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I do not think it can be said that the principle of British justice was ever based on the theory that the government or the crown would be fair to an accused person. I realize that in modern legislation, particularly in the regulations being made from time to time, the old theory of protecting the accused is being sacrificed to the principle of making it convenient for the crown, not necessarily to convict but to prosecute. It seems to me that, if the crown authorities desire, under the provisions of subsection 6 they could try a man, perhaps 600 or 700 miles from where he lives, from where his witnesses might be or from where his records might be. It may be said that that is fantastic, that no government would be so unfair, but I repeat that British criminal jurisdiction has not been built on the foundation of trusting the crown authorities; it has been based on the rights of an accused person, on the principle that his rights will never be infringed. Those battles for liberty of the person and the right to make a full and free defence were fought long ago, and the onus or a heavy part of the burden has always rested on the crown. It should not be made easy for the crown to proceed at the expense of an accused person. I suggest that we should get back to the theory of protecting the accused, and therefore the amendment moved by the hon. member for Kamloops should be accepted by the government or carried by this committee.
Amendment (Mr. Fulton) negatived.
P.C. 3 as amended agreed t.o.
On P.C. 245.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I think it would be a mistake to let this opportunity pass without driving one more nail into the coffin.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Where will you get it from?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I have been told where I can get one to finish the job if I can just hit the nail on the head. There are two schools of thought in connection with this scarcity of nails. One is that the fault lies with the manufacturers, and the other is that there is a bottleneck at the wholesale level. I agree with the hon. member for Kamloops that it is impossible for the retail trade to secure nails.
It should be emphasized that not only is it difficult to secure nails for construction purposes but, as has been indicated from my riding, it is difficult to obtain them for other purposes. A fish-box manufacturer at Penetang has had his factory closed down for six months because of a lack of nails, with the result that 150 to 175 men have been out of work. They have made a strong appeal for nails, and they say they are willing to use any kind if they can get them to put into motion an industry which affects our entire food supply. I have had communications from the retail hardware dealers' association complaining that they are unable to obtain nails. They contend that there is a bottleneck at the wholesale level, that nails are being passed out to large users.
I consider this matter of sufficient consequence and importance that the department or the steel controller should take notice of it. The excuse is made that if more nails are manufactured there will be no wire fencing, that it is a question of deciding which is the most important. It seems to me that there has been a lack of planning. When nails were first mentioned in this house we never thought for one moment our national economy would depend on this ordinary article.
The ratepayers of the town of Meaford voted to build a new public school to cost $160,000, but they were unable to obtain the nails required to start this public building. Building, particularly in the smaller communities, will be at a standstill, while people who are building huge skyscrapers and constructing places of amusement will be able to obtain all the nails they need. I do not think it is a matter of more controls. I am one of those who believe that the controls should have been removed long ago, particularly on industries of this kind. There would then have been a greater incentive to produce. It is all right to argue about price, but if you are unable to
Emergency Powers

obtain an article at any price it creates a graver situation than if you can obtain it at some price.
It is interesting to note that those who are willing to patronize the black market are able to secure these items that should be sold through the regular trade channels. It must be accepted that it is the controls which drive legitimate dealers to carry on through the black market. This evidence was well supported by the minister of reconstruction when he stated, in effect, in this house that they had discovered there were more used cars being sold through the black market than through any other source and that for that reason controls were being removed.
I think wTe shall have to grapple with this problem in some realistic manner in order to meet the demands of those engaged in the construction industry and the production of goods and services so necessary to the general economic welfare of the country. I wanted to put these remarks on the record even though nails have been spoken of so often. However I think this is the first time I have mentioned them in the house. I do hope that the steel controller and those charged with responsibility will give immediate consideration to one of the greatest problems we have to contend with at the present time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I want to get a little information, and perhaps I might even get that causeway built across the strait of Canso before I am finished. I am sorry the minister of reconstruction is not in his place at the moment, but I shall leave a few thoughts with his parliamentary assistant. During the last war the federal government rehabilitated a plate mill at Sydney, Nova Scotia. That mill had been built by the Canadian government at the time of the first war at a cost of $11,000,000 to the taxpayers of Canada. It did not go into production because the war was finished before it was ready. My information is that the company sued the government for breach of contract because the mill did not produce and they secured some more money.
During the period between the two wars all the machinery from that mill was moved by the then existing corporation to Ojibway in Ontario. When the last war broke out, all that *was left was the shell of that mill which had been erected at a cost of $11,000,000 to the taxpayers of Canada. I raised the matter on several occasions in 1940, and finally the present minister of reconstruction made a statement to the house that the government intended to rehabilitate the mill. This meant that 
for the second time the taxpayers of Canada would equip the mill at Sydney and put it into production.
During a part of this war that mill employed some 600 men and produced steel plate for shipbuilding purposes. As soon as the wrar ended, the mill went out of production and it stands idle today in Sydney, Nova Scotia. The federal government has been requested by the city council and other bodies in Nova Scotia to do something about putting that mill back into production. I wrote the minister asking whether it could not be used for the production of steel plate; and only a few days ago, on April 11 to be exact, he informed me quite definitely by letter that the mill was not going back into production. The general manager of the Sydney steel plant, Mr. C. M. Anson, replied to the inquiry of the city council as to whether this mill might be put back into production, and this is what he said:
. . . in his reply to the council advised that the plate mill was obsolete and too costly to operate in comparison with the modernly equipped mills in Upper Canada.
I would draw to the attention of the committee the fact that in 1941 this mill was reequipped by the Canadian government, and I would ask the minister or his parliamentary assistant to inform the committee whether the work done at that time and the equipment put into the mill were supervised by representatives of the government, and what kind of equipment wras put in that became Obsolete and out of date within four years, as far as the production of steel plate is concerned. Or did the government merely provide the money and allow the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation to put old, obsolete equipment in that mill, with the government paying first-class prices? My reason for asking the question is that the taxpayers of Canada have an investment of approximately 16,000,000 in that mill. At the present time we are importing most of our steel plate from the United States. There is a serious unemployment problem in that end of Canada. Is it the intention of the government to try to use that mill and put it back into production? If not, since the Canadian government and the taxpayers of Canada own that mill, will the government consider selling the mill to people I have in mind, who might put it into production?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I am sorry I am not in a position 'to give the hon. member full information on the subject. On one point, however, I can do so; that is, we will consider an offer to sell very quickly and thoroughly. As to the other part, I believe it worked out

Emergency Powers
in this way; that it was the rehabilitation of an old plant which was not equipped. That was done by the company, but they obtained a loan for the purpose from the dominion government. Part of the loan was repaid; a settlement was then made, and the plant was turned over to the crown in settlement of certain balances outstanding. I believe that is the way in which the transaction was carried out. With my lack of information I do not think it would be useful for me to extend my remarks on the subject.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
I was perhaps the first in this house to inquire about nails something over a year ago. I am still inquiring about nails, and it seems to me that the answer given tonight was no better than the answer given a year ago in regard to the nail situation. I do not believe the answer which has been given is good enough, and I think the government should do something immediately to see that nails are made available to the people of Canada, not only for building purposes but for urgent repairs on the farm. If only fifteen per cent of the nails produced are being held on priority for housing purposes, where are the rest of the nails going? I believe the people of Canada should be given an answer to that question. Especially do I think something should be done for the farmers. Here is a quotation from a letter from a hardware dealer, showing what happens when farmers come in and ask for nails:
As a parting shot the farmer customer will venture the assertion that "had the farmers been as completely indifferent to the appeals of the government during wartime, as the government now is to the needs of the farmer, a totally different production picture would have resulted." He will further state that in his humble opinion the primary industry of the nation should at least have some consideration.
The farmer today is still being asked to produce the things we need so badly. During the war he had to let his buildings and his equipment go.. Now, when he may have a chance to repair them, he cannot get a nail in the hardware store. I believe it is time nails were made available, somehow or another, to hardware stores, so that the farmers and the people of Canada generally who need nails so badly may procure them.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
This nail subject has been going on now ever since I hit the nail on the head in the Citizen on Friday, and I believe enough pressure has been brought to bear on the government. At least we have been told by the parliamentary assistant that the steel controller is looking over the situation in western Canada. I am as anxious as anyone else to pass the rest of the orders in council
so that we may hear the budget tomorrow night. It does not matter whether we talk on this subject for another two days; enough light has been thrown on it now, and I believe the minister is taking steps to remedy the situation at once.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: We have heard about nails tonight, and we heard about nails last week. I remember that in answering some members on this side the minister made the statement that today nails are under the control of private enterprise. It has been suggested several times this evening that there is a black market in nails. I do not know whether or not that is true, but if it is there is only one source nails can come from; that is, from the people who make them. We have just passed P.C. 3, which gives the minister all kinds of power to examine books, sales and so on. I would suggest that the government examine the books of the firms making nails to find out whether or not there is a black market, and if there is, that it should take the necessary action to see that this practice ceases.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

I have forgotten, Mr. Chairman, whether I was at a comma or a semicolon when being ruled out of order a few minutes ago; therefore I had better start over. Under this order in council I wish to say a few words with respect to the situation regarding supplies of lumber in Nova Scotia. My point in this regard was raised as a result of the statement made on April 22, 1947, by the Minister of Reconstruction andi Supply. In that statement he said that the retail price of lumber in internal British Columbia and in the prairie provinces was to be raised to encourage the production of lumber. I believe that regulation does not apply east of Manitoba.
The Nova Scotian situation with respect to the supply of lumber is somewhat unique as is Nova Scotia's situation with respect to the supply and availability of a good many products. With regard to lumber we have what one might call a three-cornered situation. There is practically no demand in central or western Canada for Nova Scotian lumber. There is a great foreign demand, but in this direction the amount of export is limited by the amount of lumber put on the domestic market. In the local domestic field we are also limited in the amount of lumber we can put on the market, because of the retail prices. Our retail dealers, who form a substantial part of our economy in lumber, are forced, if they adhere to the ceiling, to put lumber on the local domestic market at a loss. With the export market limited and in some cases unavailable to retailers, there is a definite limit as to how far these retailers can or will go in serving the public at a loss.
From the discussion in the committee one would gather that there is a substantial market in Canada for lumber produced in Nova Scotia. In fact, when the hon. member for Davenport earlier this evening mentioned the manufacture of prefabricated houses in Quebec I could have said that in Nova Scotia also we have manufactured a substantial number of prefabricated houses of the same type. It is true they were for emergency shelter. They did not contain any of the normal conveniences except wiring. Wiring was supplied

Emergency Powers
in the form of a kit. However they were quite good houses; they were made for the export market and I understand that they served the purpose well. In Nova Scotia we have tried our best to interest the Canadian government in purchasing these houses, particularly after seeing in papers all over Canada that there was an urgent demand for emergency shelter. But we have never been successful in having any of these prefabricated houses used elsewhere in Canada. Therefore, because there is no demand for our lumber products elsewhere in Canada, we look to the local domestic market and here we are restricted by the selling price. We are limited on the export market, where there is a great demand, by the quota system. We feel that we are squeezed from, all sides.
There is a further aspect with respect to British Columbia fir, which is almost totally unavailable for private enterprise. Recently, through the good offices of the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply and the timber controller, we have been able to get a fair allocation for all government projects, but for private projects Douglas fir is simply not available, and that in itself is quite a restraint on production and construction. It has happened, as it has happened elsewhere in Canada, that the ceiling price on lumber has not been too carefully adhered to ini many instances, with the result that lumber is not as easy to get as it might be because of black market dealings; but I believe that the availability is increasing. The Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island lumber dealers' association met last week, and in a press report (he following appeared:
A committee, appointed by the association, to study the supply and distribution of certain commodities, reported they were highly satisfied with the results achieved thus far and a very cooperative spirit had been displayed by the manufacturers.
On the other hand, in the same report of the association's proceedings it was stated:
Most members reported that lumber stocks *were down to a minimum and it continued difficult to build up an inventory, particularly in spruce. Doors and hardwood flooring were also in short supply as well as cedar shingles, wood lath and other building materials.
I have heard from lumber dealers that the situation is easing and that the distribution is good. My own limited experience is to the effect that the situation internally is easing. So that in the light of the minister's announcement with respect to western Canada and our own particular situation in Nova Scotia and, I believe, in Prince Edward Island-I think I am safe in saying that, having regard to the fact that the meeting I referred to 83166-161
was a joint meeting of the Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island lumber dealers' association-we are now at the point where one of three things should be done, probably jointly in some instances. First of all, if there is an over-all shortage in Canada there should be a greater opportunity for putting our lumber and lumber products at a profit on Canadian markets other than the maritimes. Second, the time, I believe, is arriving, if it has not already arrived, when the domestic ceiling price should be raised. Third, I believe the time is at hand when full consideration should be given to increasing export quotas, and I should be pleased to hear the parliamentary assistant make some statement in that regard.

I want to second what has been said by the hon. member (Mr. Winters) with reference to maritime lumber. He spoke particularly about Nova Scotia, but what he said would apply, I believe, with even greater force to New Brunswick. The lumber dealers and people generally in New Brunswick are greatly interested in the lumber industry, because it supplies work for nearly one-third of our people. The people there were greatly concerned at the report of the minister a few days ago that the price of domestic lumber from British Columbia and in the prairie provinces was to be increased from fifteen to twenty per cent. Our people in my own province and, I am satisfied, in other maritime provinces, are at a loss to understand why there should be an increase in domestic lumber from fifteen to twenty per cent from British Columbia and the west and not from the maritime provinces as well. I sometimes wonder whether British Columbia has more pull with this government than we from the maritime provinces have. As I listened tonight and heard the minister from British Columbia, and all the members from that province, join forces in the matter of housing in the city of Vancouver, the thought occurred to me that where there is unity there is strength; and possibly it is in this unity which we find among the members from British Columbia that their strength lies. I would suggest to my colleagues from the maritimes-and I do so in all sincerity-that we from the maritimes should take a lesson from British Columbia members, and in matters of this kind, when they affect our provinces, we should all stand together, irrespective of whether we are opposition or government members and try to see that whatever government is in power, whether Liberal or Conservative, shall do justice to our section of

I am quite sincere. This is a serious matter to my own province and to show how serious it is, I have here a newspaper item in the Saint John Telegraph-Journal of Saturday of this week, the heading being "Timber controls threaten our lumber industry." In other words, the timber controls threaten the industry in the province of New Brunswick.
I am sorry the minister himself is not here tonight, because I should like him to tell me just why there is this discrimination, and it is rank and unfair discrimination, that we are getting in New Brunswick and' other maritime provinces today in respect of lumber. The minister is a very busy man and I -am not reflecting on his not being here, because he is here on all occasions when it is possible for him to attend, and if he is away tonight I am satisfied it is for a good reason. However I wish he were here tonight to answer that question why there is this discrimination.
The hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg pointed out just why the lumber industry and why the controls have a great effect on our maritime industry. He said we mostly export our lumber, and that is a fact. Some years ago, I believe it was under the empire trade agreements, we exported our lumber for the most part to Great Britain. We developed a splendid market there, and anyone who has been in the port of Halifax or Saint John or in any of the other ports in the maritime provinces and seen in the past ten -or twelve years ships loading for the British market will realize what a splendid industry it is. But what are these controls doing as far as our industry is concerned?
It was pointed out that we have a small quota, and today we see the hand, not of the British Columbia politician, but at least of the lumber industry of that province. The quota

for export lumber is controlled) mostly by British Columbia and we in the maritime provinces have a very small quota. We are allowed to ship lumber to the United States, but for every carload of lumber that is shipped across the border in to the United States we must sell two carloads in Canada. There is a price ceiling on our lumber, and I am told on good authority-other members from -the maritime provinces can correct me if I am wrong-that the price ceiling on lumber produced in the maritimes is $8 less than cost of production. When, therefore, a lumber exporter sends his one car of lumber to the United States or his quota to Great Britain he has to make enough on that exported lumber to pay his loss on lumber sold on the domestic market.
What is the effect of this? Well, the effect is this. We are asking high prices from countries to which we export and we are asking a high price in the British market. We are taking advantage today of the people in Great Britain in their great famine for lumber. We are taking advantage of them in making them pay for the loss we sustain in this country in selling lumber -below cost of production. There is no question about that, and we in New Brunswick and in the other maritime provinces feel that this will have a detrimental effect on future trade, this great business which has been worked up over a long period of years. What are the people of Great Britain going to say in years to come when they can get lumber in other parts of the world instead of from Canada and the maritime provinces? They will say, "In the time of our greatest need, when you should have sold us lumber cheaper than you did, you took advantage of our stress and sold it at prices much higher than you were selling in your own country". The result will be, I am sure, that when Russia gets back on her feet, when great exporting countries get back, when Finland is exporting to Great Britain and when Sweden is again shipping lumber, we shall lose that splendid market in Great Britain in consequence of what they regard as the unfair treatment which we gave them in the time of their greatest need.
You speak about black markets. I am satisfied that there is a black market in lumber in the maritime provinces. As I said, the price of lumber is $8 below the cost of production. The natural result of that is that the producer is going to hold the lumber and sell it at the highest price, if it is at all possible. It is being done, and it is being done in a widespread manner. You talk about a black market in nails. There is a black market in lumber, I think, not only in the maritime provinces but here in Ontario. The reason

Emergency Powers
is that we are selling lumber in this country-today at below cost of production. In discussing this lumber situation, and particularly our loss of foreign markets and foreign customers, the Telegraph-Journal had this to say on April 26:
This is unfair to our foreign customers.
It is doubly unfair to our producers. On one hand, they are strong-armed into selling in Canada at a loss-a thing which is almost incomprehensible and is certainly not in accord with sound business practice or sound government administration. On the other hand, they see their foreign markets being shattered by a shortsighted and ruthless policy.
They know how stiff competition is under ordinary conditions. Here in New Brunswick, for instance, they have seen lack of markets knock the bottom out of prices, throw thousands of workers out of jobs, and drive wages in the woods and mills down to a shocking and pitiful level.
That statement, Mr. Chairman, is correct; and I am sure it is a well-considered statement. I should also like to quote from the Telegraph-Journal of February 15, and that is some months ago. This was not only the feeling a few days ago when this regulation was changed, but for many months the people in the maritime provinces have felt that these controls and regulations were most unfair to our lumber industry, which is the most, important one we have in our province. On February 15 of this year, the Telegraph-Journal had this to say:
Our timber trade with Great Britain is traditional. More than that, it is essential to our prosperity. Our position, if we lost it. would be utterly hopeless. Yet today men who are ignorant of the timber trade are in the driver's seat and . . . are -whipping this vital industry toward destruction. This we can't afford to tolerate.
The same article goes on to refer to other commodities that we are selling to Great Britain. Take wheat, for instance. We are not selling wheat to Great Britain at a much higher price than we are selling it in. this country. We realized that the people of Great Britain needed wheat and needed it badly. The policy we adopted was this, that we sell wheat to Great Britain as cheaply as we possibly can in order to help those people who so much need our help. Why dlo we have one policy for lumber, as to which there is also a famine in Great Britain, and another policy for wheat?
There were many other things that I had intended to say, Mr. Chairman, but I see that it is nearly eleven o'clock and I shall take only a few more minutes of the committee's time. I thought possibly the hon. member for Lunenburg might have mentioned the situation with regard to birch woods in the maritime provinces. We have in the maritime 83166-161i
provinces almost a billion feet of birch wood lumber which today we are not able to cut and export. Why? Because our quota will not allow us to do that. What is happening to this -birch wood lumber? There is a disease known as dieback disease, which is gradually wiping out all these birch wood forests. In five years' time, we are told, all this splendid birch wood will be ruined and will not be fit to export unless a special quota is given to the maritime provinces and we are allowed to cut and export this birch wood. Because of controls and the quota, what is happening? We are not allowed to cut it. It is going to waste. Yet it is worth millions of dollars to us. It gives employment to thousands of our men. In spite of the fact that Mr. MacQuarrie, minister of lands and mines of Nova Scotia, has made special representations to this government, no extra quota has been given, and this great loss has been inflicted on the people of Nova Scotia and the people of New Brunswick.
Mr. Chairman, I will take no more of the time of the committee, but I hope that the minister will reconsider the treatment which he has given to the maritime provinces and will endeavour to correct what we consider to be very great wrongs.
Progress reported.
